Dans les coulisses des concerts de Céline Dion à Paris : comment a été fabriquée sa spectaculaire robe noire Dior ? Céline Dion en Dior ce 25 septembre à la Plenitude Arena à Paris. - Thomas Chéné C’est bien simple, en ce moment, la planète n’a plus qu’un seul prénom à la bouche : Céline. Comme on l’attendait, son grand retour a pris des allures de raz-de-marée absolu. Évidemment, pour ses retrouvailles avec la scène parisienne après six ans d’absence, la diva n’a pas fait les choses à moitié. Le 25 septembre dernier, face aux 35.000 spectateurs en transe de la Plenitude Arena, Céline Dion est apparue dès les premières notes de son tube On ne change pas , moulée dans une création sur mesure Dior signée Jonathan Anderson . Chaque apparition de la chanteuse est désormais attendue comme un statement mode ausculté sous toutes les coutures. Et cette fois encore, ça n’a pas loupé. À lire aussi Clefs Michelin : trois nouveaux hôtels belges rejoignent le palmarès Instagram DdzT6rYCCSm Au premier coup d’œil, une longue colonne de mousseline noire minimaliste. Une coupe qui épouse parfaitement la ligne de la star avant de basculer dans le spectacle : d’imposants éventails de crin plissé noir et gris clair, entièrement rebrodés de cristaux et de perles, viennent sculpter la taille. Sur le côté, une basque théâtrale vient casser la verticalité pour offrir à la pièce ce mouvement fascinant, oscillant entre fleur géante et pièce d’architecture. Presque sage de face, infiniment plus audacieuse de profil. Pas besoin d’une traîne de dix mètres ni d’une orgie de strass pour régner sur l’arena. Ici, la puissance réside dans la construction. On a infiltré le Brussels Stephex Masters qui rassemble la crème mondiale de l’équitation Jonathan Anderson fouille dans les archives Dior Pour concevoir cette pièce, Jonathan Anderson est allé fureter dans les archives du 30 Avenue Montaigne, exhumant la robe Francis Poulenc, chef-d’œuvre haute couture dessiné par Christian Dior pour sa collection printemps-été 1950 (la mythique ligne Verticale). 76 ans plus tard, Anderson extrait le concept du plissé poétique et la silhouette florale, mais dépoussière l’ensemble : les volumes deviennent asymétriques, la palette se resserre sur un duo noir et gris souverain, et la jupe ample cède sa place à une colonne acérée, presque graphique. Ce jeu de miroir avec le passé est d’ailleurs devenu la marque de fabrique du Dior de Jonathan Anderson. Le créateur irlandais est passé maître dans l’art de télescoper patrimoine et tension contemporaine. Instagram Céline et Dior, une vieille histoire Alors sur Céline Dion, l’exercice prend presque une dimension mythologique. Car l’histoire d’amour entre la star québécoise et la maison parisienne est une suite ininterrompue de coups d’éclat. À commencer par les Oscars 1999, lorsqu’elle osait le smoking blanc porté à l’envers par John Galliano. Un coup de poker moqué par la presse à l’époque, et devenu aujourd’hui un moment d’anthologie. Au milieu des années 2010, Céline Dion opère l’un des virages stylistiques les plus réjouissants de la pop culture. Avec Law Roach aux commandes, ses sorties parisiennes deviennent des mini-défilés sauvages. Elle enfile une robe Balenciaga vert acide signée Demna, du Off-White de Virgil Abloh, des cuissardes, des silhouettes couture impossibles à porter pour le commun des mortels. Au Met Gala de 2019 consacré au « camp », elle ne se contente pas de comprendre le thème, mais l’avale tout cru. Oscar de la Renta lui confectionne une spectaculaire silhouette de showgirl inspirée des Ziegfeld Follies, ruisselante de franges perlées, coiffée d’un couvre-chef de plumes pesant près de dix kilos. De la tour Eiffel à la Plenitude Arena Dior, pendant ce temps, n’a jamais été très loin. On la retrouve en total look de la maison au premier rang de la haute couture dès 2016, puis en Christian Dior Resort dans les rues de Paris en 2017. Mais leur autre grand rendez-vous reste évidemment juillet 2024. Affaire Cornell : la gouverneure de New York veut changer la loi sur les victimes de viol en état d’ébriété REUTERS. L a gouverneure de l’Etat de New York, Kathy Hochul, a promis vendredi de réformer une loi polémique qui rend difficile pour une victime de faire reconnaître un viol si elle avait consommé au préalable de l’alcool ou des stupéfiants de son plein gré. Le fait d’être en état d’ébriété ou sous l’emprise de drogues après une consommation volontaire « ne donne pas licence pour une agression sexuelle ou un viol en réunion », a déclaré l’élue en référence à ce texte qui fait écho à une affaire impliquant des étudiants de l’université Cornell. Violée par sept étudiants Le procureur du comté de Tompkins (nord de l’Etat de New York), où se trouve le campus, a annoncé lundi la réouverture d’une enquête sur un viol en réunion présumé remontant à octobre 2024, après qu’une jeune femme a saisi la justice civile. Agée de 20 ans au moment des faits, elle affirme avoir été violée par sept étudiants, tous membres de la fraternité Chi Phi, alors qu’elle avait consommé de l’alcool et de la kétamine. À lire aussi Gisèle Pelicot, l’art de se reconstruire sur un champ de ruines L’affaire a déclenché une vague d’indignation, sur le campus de Cornell et au-delà, beaucoup la considérant comme emblématique d’une culture liée aux fraternités dans les universités. Le procureur Matthew Van Houten, qui était déjà en fonction en 2024, a expliqué ne pas avoir donné suite à une première plainte car les éléments transmis par la police faisaient état, selon lui, de rapports consensuels. Selon plusieurs médias, la police aurait expurgé une partie de la déposition de la plaignante dans laquelle elle qualifiait les faits de viol et assurait avoir été contrainte. Jeudi, Kathy Hochul a désigné la procureure de l’Etat de New York Letitia James comme procureure spéciale chargée de l’enquête. La démocrate, qui a notamment mené des investigations contre Donald Trump, s’est engagée à « examiner les faits, rassembler les preuves, interroger les témoins et, si cela est justifié, engager des poursuites ». « Je suis favorable à changer cette loi » « Si quelqu’un est trop diminué » par les effets de l’alcool, des stupéfiants ou des deux, « le fait que la consommation ait été volontaire ou non ne devrait pas entrer en compte », a martelé Kathy Hochul. « Je suis favorable à changer cette loi et je vais travailler avec le Parlement de New York pour y parvenir », a-t-elle annoncé. Une proposition de loi avait déjà été déposée en ce sens l’an dernier par l’élu à la chambre basse de l’Etat de New York Jeffrey Dinowitz. « Régulièrement, des procureurs sont dans l’incapacité de poursuivre des agresseurs sexuels (présumés) à cause de cette lacune dans les textes », a souligné cet élu sur X. Près de vingt Etats américains sont régis par des textes similaires. Plusieurs autres ont modifié leur législation ces dernières années, notamment le Texas, en 2025, inspiré par le cas d’une ancienne étudiante de l’université du Texas violée dix ans plus tôt lors d’une fête organisée par une fraternité. Nations League: Italy reel in France to spoil Zidane's homecoming party. Italy ended Zinedine Zidane's triumphant start as France head coach on Friday night with a 1-1 draw at the Stade de France in the Uefa Nations League.

Culture versus climate: how global heating endangers Unesco heritage sites. Unesco World Heritage sites in France and around the world are under threat from the climate crisis. From ancient cities to medieval abbeys, floods, droughts, rising seas and wildfires are putting humanity’s most precious cultural heritage at risk.

Ethiopia's government forces look to take regional capital from Tigray rebels. Tigray rebels are abandoning their regional capital in northern Ethiopia, local residents said on Saturday, as pro-government forces advanced on the city. It marks a win for the federal government as it seeks to drive back a rebel offensive, which has triggered the worst fighting in the region since the civil war of 2020-2022.

All hail Queen Céline as pop diva hits halfway mark in Paris comeback. Canadian singer Céline Dion has reached the halfway point in her marathon of 16 concerts in Paris, marking her big return to the stage after years away. As she works to overcome the effects of a debilitating illness, fans and professionals say the star is not only a music legend, but a fashion icon to boot.

Crise du logement en Espagne: le Parlement rejette deux textes, revers cuisant pour Pedro Sanchez. C'est un échec pour Pedro Sanchez : les deux textes présentés devant le Parlement pour résoudre la crise du logement ont été rejetés, vendredi 2 octobre, par les députés, malgré la mobilisation de plus en plus importante dans la rue en Espagne pour réclamer justement des mesures en faveur des locataires. Si le chef du gouvernement espagnol espérait obtenir le soutien des députés dans cette crise majeure, il en a été tout autrement.

Ligue des nations: Zidane retrouve le Stade de France, les Bleus butent sur la Squadra Azzurra. Ce vendredi 2 octobre, Zinédine Zidane faisait ses retrouvailles avec le public tricolore au Stade de France, en tant que sélectionneur des Bleus. Après deux rencontres gagnées en Ligue des nations en Turquie puis en Belgique, la France a concédé le nul face à l'Italie (1-1). Michael Olise a ouvert le score en seconde période, Alessandro Bastoni lui a répondu.

Faut-il croire Mediapart après ses révélations sur les propos antisémites attribués à Jordan Bardella?. Ce sont des informations fracassantes qui bousculent le début de campagne, à quelques mois de la présidentielle en France. Le journal en ligne Mediapart a été, cette semaine, au centre de révélations sur le passé antisémite de Jordan Bardella. Pourtant, le président du Rassemblement national nie les propos qui lui sont attribués.

Centrafrique: avec le football, «on oublie la guerre et les armes» à Birao [2/3]. À Birao, dans l'extrême nord-est de la République centrafricaine, le sport, et particulièrement le football, se pratique dans des conditions extrêmement difficiles. Le manque criant d'infrastructures et d'équipements freine le développement des sportifs, malgré l'existence de nombreux talents.

Blocage des lycées en France: les organisations lycéennes et étudiantes appellent à un «acte 3» le 6 octobre. Alors que le mouvement des lycéens n'a cessé de s'étendre durant toute la semaine et qu'il a donné lieu à des actions parfois violentes, trois syndicats de lycéens ont été reçus par le ministre de l'Éducation nationale, Édouard Geffray, vendredi 2 octobre. Déçus par les mesures proposées, ils appellent à la poursuite de la mobilisation.

Éthiopie: une milice alliée au gouvernement fédéral revendique la prise de l'aéroport de Mekele. Faite sur le réseau social X, l'annonce intervient alors que les Forces de paix du Tigré (TPF) ont déjà repris le contrôle de plusieurs localités du sud du Tigré ces derniers jours. L'aéroport de Mekele avait été pris le 23 septembre dernier par le Front de libération du peuple du Tigré (TPLF), au début de l'offensive lancée par la nouvelle alliance d’opposition hostile au gouvernement fédéral.

Guinée: le président Mamadi Doumbouya gracie l'opposant Aliou Bah. Plusieurs dizaines de prisonniers condamnés se sont vus accorder une remise totale de peine à l'occasion de la fête nationale guinéenne, vendredi 2 octobre. Parmi eux figure notamment l'opposant Aliou Bah, qui avait été arrêté fin 2024 et condamné en mai 2025 à deux ans de prison pour « offense et diffamation » envers le chef de l'État.

Yémen: la ville de Taëz, enjeu majeur des combats entre Houthis et forces gouvernementales. Les combats s’intensifient au Yémen entre les rebelles Houthis et les forces gouvernementales soutenues par l’Arabie saoudite. Alors que la milice pro-iranienne accuse Riyad d’avoir bombardé le pays à plus de 90 reprises - notamment la capitale Sanaa - vendredi 2 octobre, de violents affrontements ont également fait des dizaines de morts dans la région de Taëz, située entre Aden et les positions des Houthis.

«Au bord du précipice»: à Kiev, les frappes russes sur les ponts perturbent fortement la circulation. En Ukraine, la Russie poursuit ses frappes contre Kiev et vise désormais les ponts qui relient les deux rives de la ville. Dans la nuit du jeudi 1er au vendredi 2 octobre, le pont sud a ainsi été touché, provoquant de fortes perturbations pour ceux qui ont l'habitude de traverser le Dnipro en métro ou en voiture. Un chaos routier qui devrait se poursuivre tout le week-end et constitue une nouvelle épreuve pour les habitants de la capitale.

Lettonie: qui sortira vainqueur des législatives, entre menace russe et tensions économiques?. Ce samedi, c'est jour d'élection en Lettonie. Le scrutin pour composer le Parlement se déroule alors que la menace russe est palpable dans ce pays balte. La Lettonie, qui accueille des dizaines de milliers de réfugiés ukrainiens et est fortement engagée dans le soutien à l'Ukraine, subit des incursions de drones et reçoit des vagues de demandeurs d'asile venus du Moyen-Orient ou d'Afrique subsaharienne, poussés vers l'Europe depuis la Biélorussie voisine, alliée de Moscou. Le tout dans un contexte économique délicat.

Biélorussie: quatre journalistes libérés, 17 autres toujours détenus. Quatre journalistes biélorusses ont retrouvé la liberté le 16 septembre dernier, à la faveur d’une amnistie obtenue grâce à l’intervention de la diplomatie américaine. Mais leur libération a immédiatement été suivie d’une expulsion et d’un exil forcé. Si Reporters sans frontières (RSF) salue ces libérations, l’organisation dénonce le maintien en détention de 17 autres journalistes et professionnels des médias, toujours incarcérés en Biélorussie.

Élections au Brésil: le duel Lula-Bolsonaro, un air de déjà vu. Un scrutin décisif se joue au Brésil dimanche 4 octobre. Dans ce pays fortement polarisé, la gauche de l’actuel président Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva est aux coudes-à-coudes face à l’extrême droite de Flávio Bolsonaro, fils de l’ex-président Jair Bolsonaro. Deux visions du Brésil et de sa place à l’international s’opposent.

Inde: «Ce n'est qu'un début», la mobilisation se poursuit contre la fraude électorale. En Inde, la mobilisation des jeunes se poursuit face à la crise qui touche le système électoral. Les syndicats étudiants ont appelé à de nouvelles manifestations samedi, tandis que les partis politiques se mettent en ordre de marche pour engager un bras de fer avec le pouvoir. Au centre des tensions, la Commission électorale qui a radié environ 130 millions de citoyens des listes électorales. Elle est accusée de favoriser ainsi le BJP, le parti du Premier ministre Narendra Modi

La couleur comme ancêtre: le photographe Rafael Pavarotti célèbre l'«amefricanité» à Paris. Le musée des Arts décoratifs de Paris consacre jusqu'au 2 mai 2027 une exposition au photographe Rafael Pavarotti. Né en Amazonie et nourri des cultures afro-autochtones du Brésil, il a conquis la mode et la pop culture par ses couleurs vibrantes et son style théâtral. Des géants du luxe à Beyoncé, en passant par Madonna, avec qui il a étroitement collaboré pour son dernier album, tous ont succombé à son esthétique.

Irak: les avocats de Français accusés de jihadisme «interdits» de territoire par Badgad. Quatorze Français, soupçonnés d'avoir appartenu à l'État islamique et détenus en Irak pour jihadisme, doivent être jugés par la justice irakienne. Après plusieurs audiences procédurales, les premiers procès doivent débuter lundi. Les accusés risquent la peine de mort, alors que leurs avocats ont appris vendredi par le Quai d'Orsay leur interdiction de territoire irakien. Ces derniers pointent le manque de réaction de la France.

Indonésie: l'éruption de l'Anak Krakatoa pourrait être à l’origine de l’apparition de deux nouvelles îles. En Indonésie, l’éruption d’un volcan pourrait bien être à l’origine de l’apparition de deux nouvelles îles. Les autorités du pays ont annoncé vendredi 2 octobre avoir découvert deux nouvelles étendues de terre à proximité du volcan Anak Krakatoa. Son éruption début septembre avait entraîné la fermeture de nombreux aéroports du pays.

Huit ans après l'assassinat de Jamal Khashoggi, ses proches dénoncent la complaisance envers le régime saoudien. Le 2 octobre 2018, le journaliste saoudien Jamal Khashoggi, critique régulier de la monarchie saoudienne dans ses écrits, en particulier dans le Washington Post, trouvait la mort, assassiné selon la CIA par des agents saoudiens sur ordre du prince héritier Mohammed ben Salmane, provoquant l'indignation de la communauté internationale. Huit ans plus tard les proches de Jamal Khashoggi se sont rassemblés à Washington pour dénoncer l'impunité dont bénéficie MBS et son retour en grâce dans les cercles diplomatiques occidentaux.

Édouard Philippe essaie de ne pas buter sur les retraites. Édouard Philippe a enfin présenté cette semaine son projet de réforme des retraites. Le candidat Horizons à la présidentielle était très attendu sur cette question sensible depuis qu'il avait évoqué la possibilité de fixer l'âge de départ à 67 ans. Finalement, il place la barre à 65 ans mais sa réforme reste orientée vers la recherche d'économies avec des mesures difficiles, au risque de ne pas faire adhérer les Français.

Au Brésil, l'influence du crime organisé sur l'élection présidentielle dans les favelas de Rio. Au Brésil, les électeurs sont appelés aux urnes dimanche pour le premier tour de la présidentielle qui oppose notamment le sortant Lula à Flavio Bolsonaro, fils de l'ex-président d'extrême droite. Une élection sous l'influence du crime organisé, entre candidats en lien avec des groupes mafieux ou criminels, achats de votes, ou encore pressions sur les électeurs, comme dans les favelas de Rio de Janeiro.

Vol Flydubai pour Tel-Aviv: l'enquête émiratie établit que le copilote planifiait un «acte terroriste». Le procureur général des Émirats arabes unis a indiqué que l'enquête sur le vol de Flydubai avait révélé que le copilote planifiait un « acte terroriste », et avait utilisé la hache de secours du cockpit pour attaquer le pilote, a rapporté samedi l'agence de presse officielle (WAM).

États-Unis: ce que l'on sait de l'exécution manquée de Christa Pike dans le Tennessee. Christa Pike toujours inconsciente et placée sous ventilation artificielle dans un hôpital de Nashville, aux États-Unis. Il y a toujours pléthore de questions sans réponses après l’exécution manquée de cette femme de 50 ans par les services pénitentiaires du Tennessee. Ses avocats ont déposé plusieurs recours afin de préserver les preuves et de reconstituer le protocole médical.

Une mobilisation à travers le monde contre Syngenta, le roi des pesticides. De la Normandie au Kenya, en passant par la Suisse, le Pakistan ou l'Indonésie, des mobilisations contre les pesticides sont prévues ce samedi sur quatre continents avec une cible en particulier : le géant Syngenta. Paysans, malades, riverains appellent à se rassembler contre le numéro un mondial des pesticides.

Pourquoi la République dominicaine a interdit à la sélection haïtienne de football de jouer sur son territoire. La République dominicaine a interdit vendredi à la sélection de football d’Haïti, pays avec lequel elle partage l’île d’Hispaniola et entretient des relations tendues, de jouer sur son territoire. La veille, un incident avait eu lieu avant un match entre les deux voisins.

Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with preparing terror acts including against Nigel Farage. The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with preparing terrorist acts, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Two Iranian men charged over suspected terror plot targeting Jewish people in Manchester ahead of Yom Kippur. Two Iranian nationals have been charged over a suspected terror plot against Jewish people in Manchester.

Death row inmate unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution, lawyers say. Death row inmate Christa Pike is unconscious and on a ventilator in hospital after two failed execution attempts in Tennessee, her lawyers said.

Ticks carrying life-threatening virus living longer in UK, expert warns. Ticks carrying a severe and life-threatening virus are living for longer in the UK due to more regular heatwaves, an expert has warned.

Ten injured as car hits crowd in Australia in 'horrible incident'. Ten people have been injured, including several children, after a car drove into a crowd gathered to cheer on a rugby team on Saturday, Australian officials have said.
North Korea 'fires ballistic missile' after Seoul demands apology. North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea off its east coast on Saturday, South Korea and Japan have said.

Supermarket giant Tesco weighs shock takeover bid for Majestic Wine. Tesco is exploring a surprise move to buy Majestic Wine Group, Britain's biggest specialist wine chain - a deal which would further expand the supermarket giant's retail footprint.

Grüne nennen Freigabe der Ölreserven „politische Dummheit“ – Wüst hält Spritpreise für „Skandal“. Die Freigabe der Ölreserven sorgt für Kritik – vor allem von den deutschen Grünen. Aber auch eine Ökonomin bezweifelt, dass nun die Preise für Sprit sinken werden. NRW‑Ministerpräsident Wüst hält die aktuelle Preispolitik der Öl-Konzerne bereits für einen „Skandal“.

„Wenn man zusammen im Flieger nach Mallorca fliegt, ist egal, ob man aus dem Osten oder Westen kommt“. 36 Jahre nach der Wiedervereinigung sieht Historiker Hubertus Knabe die Unterschiede zwischen Ost- und Westdeutschland weitgehend überwunden. Die nationale Identität bleibe jedoch ein Problem.

Was der Zeitpunkt der Wechseljahre über das spätere Alzheimer-Risiko verrät. Frühe Wechseljahre beeinflussen nicht nur den Hormonhaushalt. Forscher sehen ihre Spuren im Gehirn – lange bevor sich erste Gedächtnisprobleme bemerkbar machen.

„Schlag ins Gesicht“ – Sächsisches Innenministerium löscht Post zu Berliner Linken. Nach dem juristischen Vorgehen der Berliner Linken hat das sächsische Innenministerium einen umstrittenen Beitrag zur Partei in den sozialen Medien gelöscht.

Copilot nahm Notfallaxt aus Cockpit als Waffe – 29-Jähriger hatte wegen Radikalisierung Flugverbot. Der Copilot, der den Piloten des Flydubai-Flugs nach Tel Aviv verletzt haben soll, ist US-Medien zufolge wegen Sicherheitsbedenken zuvor aus seinem früheren Job bei einer Fluggesellschaft im Oman entlassen worden. Luftfahrt-Experte Heinrich Großbongardt fasst die Entwicklungen zusammen.

Donald Trump schließt einen US-Exportstopp aus. Die G7-Staaten haben die Freigabe von 100 Millionen Barrel Öl aus ihren strategischen Reserven beschlossen. US-Präsident Donald Trump beteuerte nach der Einigung, ein Exportstopp für Diesel aus den USA sei ausgeschlossen.
„Wir brauchen eine Debatte über funktionierende Schulen“. Im Interview kritisiert Philipp Keßler, Chefredakteur der „Offenbach-Post“, die aktuelle Stadtbilddebatte und wirft der CDU Doppelmoral vor.

Hinrichtung nach zwei Giftspritzen abgebrochen – „Sie schnarcht“. Bei der ersten geplanten Hinrichtung einer Frau in Tennessee seit mehr als 200 Jahren ist es zu Komplikationen gekommen. Nach Darstellung von Christa Pikes Verteidigern lebt die 50-Jährige auch nach der Verabreichung zweier Giftspritzen noch.

Zwei neue Inseln nach Vulkanausbruch entdeckt. Auch einen Monat nach dem Ausbruch des Vulkans Anak Krakatau in Indonesien gilt eine erhöhte Alarmstufe. Wie jetzt bekannt wurde, sind in unmittelbarer Umgebung zwei neue Inseln entdeckt worden.

Finnlands Nationaltrainer macht einen Witz auf Kosten von Ronaldo – und keiner lacht. Das Zerwürfnis zwischen Cristiano Ronaldo und Trainer Jorge Jesus schlägt weiter hohe Wellen. Finnlands Nationaltrainer macht sich nun darüber lustig. Doch sein Gag geht nach hinten los.

„Lösungen statt Destruktion und Panikmache“ – Ramelow ruft in Kanzelrede zum Teilen auf. Zahlreiche Politiker warnen am Tag der Deutschen Einheit vor aktuellen Gefahren für die Demokratie. Bundestagsvizepräsident Bodo Ramelow (Linke) beklagt zudem eine Spaltung der Gesellschaft durch „asoziale Netzwerke“.

Deutsche Eurofighter schützen vor Drohnen und Luftraumverletzungen. Lettland wählt heute ein neues Parlament, überschattet von sicherheitspolitischen Sorgen: Die Nato-Verbündeten wurden um Unterstützung für eine sichere Durchführung der Abstimmung gebeten – die Bundeswehr verlegte vier Eurofighter zum Schutz des Luftraums in den Baltenstaat.

Ähnelte KZ-Kleidung – Zara zieht Halloween-Kostüm für Kinder zurück. Zara hat es schon wieder getan. Nach der Kritik an einem gelben Stern auf einem Kinderhemd, der an einen Judenstern erinnerte, brachte die spanische Modekette nun ein umstrittenes Halloween-Kostüm auf den Markt.

„Damals ist man als Amerikaner noch mit offenen Armen aufgenommen worden. Im Gegensatz zu heute“. Der Minimalist Steve Reich gilt als einer der größten Komponisten der Gegenwart. Im Interview zum 90. Geburtstag spricht er über seine jüdisch-habsburgischen Wurzeln, seine Musik zu einem Gerhard-Richter-Film und über seine Bewunderung für John Coltrane.

Urkundenfälschung – türkischer Schiri-Boss bleibt in U-Haft. Der türkische Fußball kommt nicht zur Ruhe. Nach einem Wettskandal erschüttert jetzt eine Affäre um den Vorsitzenden des Schiedsrichterausschusses den Verband. Die Vorwürfe wiegen schwer.

Ähnelte KZ-Kleidung – Zara zieht Halloween-Kostüm für Kinder zurück. Die spanische Modekette hat ein Halloween-Kostüm für Kinder aus dem Verkauf genommen, nachdem Kritiker Ähnlichkeiten zur Kluft von KZ-Häftlingen während der Nazi-Diktatur kritisiert hatten.

Elefanten kommunizieren mit Infraschall. Elefanten brummen, um sich über Kilometer hinweg zu verständigen. Mithilfe von KI haben Forscher die Infraschall-Laute entschlüsselt und typische Botschaften im Sozialleben der Tiere identifiziert.

10.000 Schritte am Tag? Darüber können viele Dreijährige nur lachen. Hartnäckig hält sich die Empfehlung, dass Erwachsene für ihre Gesundheit täglich 10.000 Schritte gehen sollen. Forscher haben nun untersucht, wie viel Vorschulkinder sich bewegen. Die Ergebnisse erstaunen in vielerlei Hinsicht

The body as a battleground: Iran's resistance etched in ink and blood. Iran death-row protester shot, tortured in custody. Iranian security forces shot death-row protester Alireza Sepahi four times during his arrest at home before subjecting him to weeks of torture in custody, according to a former cellmate who described his treatment.

Iran takes US response to cabinet, Hormuz clashes continue. Iran took a US response to its latest diplomatic proposal to cabinet, a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and two January protesters were executed among the key developments on Wednesday.

‘I never asked about regime change’: Student speaks out after El-Sayed exchange. US ‘feedback’ leaves Iran debating the price of diplomacy. Iran’s receipt of Washington’s response to its seven-point proposal for ending the Strait of Hormuz crisis has sharpened divisions in Tehran over whether to pursue further compromise or intensify pressure on the United States.

Prisoners beaten, kept in windowless cells at Isfahan prison. Prisoners in a security ward at Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan are beaten with cables and metal rods and held in overcrowded, windowless cells with poor ventilation, according to accounts provided to Iran International.

Iran links under scrutiny in separate Flydubai, UK airbase investigations. A Mossad spy in Iran: From banking infiltration to nuclear and missile sabotage. Al-Qaeda is Iran's quiet backup if the war turns, expert says. Iran’s truck repair hub feels the squeeze as work dries up. Shot in leg, forced into hiding: Iran protester recounts January crackdown. Iran court upholds film star’s jail term over post mourning protest victims. An appeals court in Tehran has upheld a one-year prison sentence for renowned actress Elnaz Shakerdoost over an Instagram story mourning people killed during January’s protests, her lawyer said Friday.

As the rial sinks, Iranians seek shelter in almost anything else. Iran denies teachers are quitting despite viral resignation videos. Iran’s Education Ministry dismissed reports of teacher resignations over working conditions and security pressure as a “rumor,” despite numerous videos of teachers announcing departures and a teachers’ council warning of a growing exodus.

Officials trade blame as Iran’s economy sinks deeper. Senior Iranian military and security officials have been photographed wearing smartwatches, drawing fresh criticism of their basic security discipline after years in which Israel has tracked and killed Iranian commanders through the devices around them.

Iranians are selling livestock, cars and furniture to pay for treatment their insurance no longer covers, and a member of parliament's health committee says the system has reached the point where falling ill can end in death rather than care.

Afrique du Sud, Algérie, Côte d’Ivoire, Égypte, Maroc : qui est prêt à jouer les plans B pour la CAN 2027 ?. Nucleon Security, la pépite qui défie les géants mondiaux de la cybersécurité. En Guinée équatoriale, une nouvelle vague d’expulsions relance le débat sur la libre circulation au sein de la Cemac. « Tous les militaires avaient déjà pris le large » : en RDC, la justice militaire se penche sur la chute de Bukavu. L’Ethiopie accuse l’Erythrée, le Soudan et l’Egypte de soutenir les rebelles. Le chef d’état-major général de l’armée éthiopienne a directement accusé, jeudi 24 septembre, les trois pays et « d’autres puissances extérieures » de soutenir la nouvelle alliance de groupes d’opposition qui mène depuis une semaine une offensive d’ampleur dans le nord du pays.

Quelques œuvres d’Hervé Yamguen. L’artiste camerounais présente ses dernières réalisations à la galerie Afikaris, à Paris. Au menu de l’exposition « Nos géographies intimes » : peintures, dessins, sculptures et masques. Jusqu’au 31 octobre.

Art contemporain d’Afrique : à Paris, Hervé Yamguen explore nos « géographies intimes ». L’artiste camerounais présente ses dernières œuvres dans la galerie Afikaris, située dans le 3ᵉ arrondissement de la capitale. Au menu de l’exposition, des peintures, dessins, sculptures et masques, reflets de ses vibrations intérieures. Jusqu’au 31 octobre.

Au Maroc, l’arrestation du maire de Tanger, suspecté de fraude électorale lors des législatives, plonge son parti, vainqueur du scrutin, dans la polémique. En poste depuis 2021, l’édile, membre du Parti authenticité et modernité, a été interpellé à Tanger, lundi 28 septembre, et placé en garde à vue. La justice le soupçonne d’avoir participé à une falsification massive de bulletins de vote.

L’Algérie, principal pays de départ de migrants vers l’Espagne. Depuis le début de l’année 2026, les Algériens sont la troisième nationalité la plus représentée parmi les entrées clandestines en Europe, après les Bangladais et les Soudanais.

L’Egypte hausse le ton face à l’Ethiopie sur le partage des eaux du Nil. Alors qu’Addis-Abeba s’enfonce à nouveau dans la guerre civile, Le Caire s’emploie à isoler diplomatiquement son voisin pour l’empêcher de contrôler unilatéralement le fleuve, dont l’Egypte dépend presque uniquement pour son approvisionnement.

Dans le nord du Nigeria, le nombre d’enlèvements augmente sous la pression de gangs criminels locaux et des djihadistes. Au moins 87 personnes ont été kidnappées samedi et dimanche dans les Etats de Zamfara et du Niger. Entre juillet 2025 et juin 2026, on dénombrait 7 825 victimes de prises d’otage, un chiffre en hausse qui fragilise le pouvoir, avant l’élection présidentielle de janvier 2027.

Au Maroc, malgré la nomination d’une première ministre, le plafond de verre demeure pour les femmes. Sur 395 députés élus au Parlement après le scrutin du 23 septembre, la représentation des femmes reste minoritaire (107) et cantonnée aux quotas. Toutefois, la nomination de Fatima Ezzahra El-Mansouri par le roi suscite l’espoir des associations féministes.

En Algérie, les députés étendent la peine de mort aux auteurs de feux de forêt. Le texte élargit également la peine capitale à de nouveaux cas d’enlèvements d’enfants accompagnés de violences graves, les autorités évoquant une recrudescence de ces actes ces dernières années.

Pourquoi l’Ethiopie replonge-t-elle dans la guerre ? Comprendre en trois minutes. Après plusieurs mois de tensions, les combats ont repris à la fin de septembre en Ethiopie entre l’armée fédérale éthiopienne et différents groupes rebelles, laissant planer la menace d’un nouveau conflit de grande ampleur. Une guerre civile avait déjà éclaté dans le pays entre 2020 et 2022.

En Egypte, l’arrestation de six journalistes d’un média d’investigation, signe de la nervosité du régime du président Al-Sissi. Ce coup de force sans précédent arrive au moment où les autorités doivent faire face à un contexte économique tendu et à des rivalités politiques qui s’aiguisent pour succéder au président Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi, au pouvoir depuis 2013.

Au Kenya, le lancement en un temps record du chantier de la raffinerie Dangote. Le magnat nigérian Aliko Dangote ambitionne de répliquer sa raffinerie de Lagos à Lamu, une région isolée face à l’océan Indien. Mercredi 30 septembre, en présence de chefs d’Etat africains, s’est tenue une cérémonie hautement politique et symbolique.

Pourquoi l’Algérie a élargi la peine de mort aux incendiaires et aux kidnappeurs d’enfants. Après les feux de forêts intenses et meurtriers de l’été, le chef de l’Etat, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a souhaité élargir le nombre de « crimes capitaux », passibles de la peine de mort. Le pays respectait pourtant un moratoire sur cette question depuis 1993.

A Johannesburg, la découverte de onze corps révèle l’ampleur des violences à l’égard des femmes. Depuis juillet, des corps de femmes nues ou à moitié nues, violemment battues, ont été retrouvés en banlieue de Johannesburg. Si la thèse du prédateur en série s’amenuise, la réalité d’une extrême violence infligée aux Sud-Africaines au quotidien s’impose.

Guerre en Ethiopie : des attaques de drones ciblent la capitale, les forces gouvernementales gagnent du terrain dans le nord du pays. Après les frappes sur Addis-Abeba mercredi soir, le gouvernement éthiopien a décidé la fermeture de son ambassade à Asmara. En réponse, l’Erythrée a rompu tous ses liens diplomatiques avec l’Ethiopie.

Sur l’île idyllique de Lamu, au Kenya, l’arrivée d’une mégaraffinerie de pétrole est vue comme une opportunité économique autant qu’un péril écologique. Le lancement en grande pompe de ce colossal chantier du groupe nigérian Dangote a eu lieu mercredi 30 septembre sur le port isolé de Lamu, face à l’océan Indien. L’île du même nom, écrin touristique et berceau de la culture swahilie, retient son souffle.

Au Burkina Faso et au Mali, les juntes veulent tirer profit de la manne aurifère. La maîtrise de la chaîne de production de l’or permet aux régimes militaires de réaffirmer leur souveraineté nationale sur les ressources naturelles.

Ebola en RDC : la pire épidémie de l’histoire du pays franchit la barre des 4 000 morts. Le pays fait face à une flambée inédite du virus mais la présence de groupes armés et la défiance d’une partie des populations locales entravent la riposte. Le chef de la diplomatie française, Jean-Noël Barrot, est sur place pour marquer le soutien de Paris aux autorités locales et aux humanitaires.

En Guinée, la grâce présidentielle accordée à l’opposant Aliou Bah, condamné pour « offense et diffamation ». Le président du Mouvement démocratique libéral est incarcéré depuis décembre 2024. Sa grâce, ainsi que celle de 216 autres détenus, a été décidée par le chef de l’Etat, Mamadi Doumbouya, à l’occasion de la fête de l’indépendance du pays, selon un décret présidentiel.

Ethiopie : les rebelles du Tigré quittent Makalé, la capitale régionale, selon un journaliste local. Les forces fédérales éthiopiennes ont avancé rapidement ces derniers jours en direction de Makalé. A ce stade, elles ne sont pas encore entrées dans la ville, a précisé le journaliste, cité par l’Agence France-Presse.

Axios said the meeting, chaired by Vice President JD Vance, was not announced by the Trump administration, and the last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran. Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine, the outlet reported. "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East.

US sanctions three persons, two charities over alleged Hamas funding The United States has issued sanctions against three individuals and two France-based charities that it said were part of a network that raised more than $2 million for Hamas, and announced six arrests. "These designations expose a sophisticated, multi‑year financing architecture that moved more than $2 million to Hamas through deceptive charitable fronts and cryptocurrency channels, demonstrating the organisation's persistent ability to adapt its fundraising mechanisms to evade detection," the US Treasury said in a statement. Those sanctioned include Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq, identified as a Hamas member who oversees the financial network and works with the group's media office. The US Justice Department said French authorities had also arrested sanctioned individuals Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid, who are linked to the France-based charities Association Baraka and Ensemble C Mieux. Both charities were also sanctioned in Friday's action. A third person, Nordine Barika, was also arrested by French authorities in the case, the DOJ said. "Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid operate from France, where they run purported charities ostensibly to raise money for humanitarian purposes to aid Gazan civilians," the US Treasury said. In the United States, authorities arrested three men for their alleged funding of Hamas through the network, the DOJ said. US authorities said the network had raised more than $2 million from 2020 to 2026, of which $1.5 million was raised after the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel. Report by AFP

Gaza aid delay causes chronic shortage of medical supplies, WHO says Getting humanitarian aid through Israel into Gaza is layered with "delay after delay", the World Health Organisation said Friday, as it decried "chronic shortages" of medical supplies. Reinhilde Van de Weerdt, the WHO's representative in the Palestinian territories, said the health situation in the Gaza Strip "remains utterly dire", with none of its hospitals fully functional. "Not enough humanitarian aid is entering Gaza, and definitely not enough to allow for a meaningful expansion and restoration of health services," she told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Jerusalem. She said Israel's approval system for medical and other humanitarian supplies was proving a major bottleneck. "It is laborious, time-consuming, with no guaranteed results," she said. Based on the WHO's latest analysis, large volumes of medical supplies wait for clearance for a median of 74 days, said Van de Weerdt, adding that if it is not, "than we start that lengthy, cumbersome process all over again". She added that the approval system kept changing, with new regulations introduced. Van de Weerdt said standard health kits used worldwide had the lowest approval rate, while X-ray machines, sterilisation equipment and spare parts for CT scans and other essential machinery "get rejected regularly". "In just the last six months alone, one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices was rejected four separate times," she said. However, medicines move "relatively well", with almost 87 percent approved and one percent rejected, she added. "It's not one single blockage. It's a system, layered with delay after delay... and on the other side of every one of these delays is a patient who is waiting," she said. "We need the unimpeded and predicable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza, at scale. Report by AFP

'Artists must pick a side': How Israel's assault on Gaza is shifting the culture on Broadway Submitted by Yasmine El-Sabawi on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 13:55 Despite a growing insistence on Palestinian rights in the theatre industry, Palestinian performers remain without a seat at the table Six months into Israel's assault on Gaza in March 2024, when more than 120 Palestinians were being killed in air strikes each day, Broadway performer Allie Trimm was approached by the writer of a project she had just been fired from. "You and I are not so different. We both don't want to see innocent people get hurt," the writer told her. "We just have a different idea of who's innocent." Trimm, an actress and singer since the age of nine, had become an advocate for Palestinian rights after images of children torn apart by US-supplied weapons flooded her social media feeds, as they had for countless other Americans since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. Just under 1,200 people - Israelis and foreign nationals - were killed that morning, including some by the Israeli military . Israel's subsequent assault on the Gaza Strip, later assessed to be a genocide by the United Nations and Holocaust scholars , has killed 74,000 Palestinians to date, with more than 22,000 children among them. Researchers with the Lancet Global Health Journal have said those figures are likely a severe undercount . Trimm told Middle East Eye that industry professionals called her a "jihadist" and "antisemite", and warned her that she was putting people in danger through her advocacy. "How is humanising Palestinian people being equated with antisemitism?" she said. "This is the first issue that I've really experienced with such intense silencing around [it], and... Well, why? Why is it this thing that we can't talk about?" 'Censorship' In November 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, and three Hamas leaders who were assassinated by Israel. The move upped the ante on Israel as international condemnation of its conduct in Gaza escalated. The US has since vowed to dismantle the ICC " brick by brick ". Trimm told MEE she wasn't employed for some nine months that year before she landed a leading role on Broadway's smash hit Wicked in 2025 - where she was previously a standby, or emergency fill-in - playing Glinda, the "good witch", now recognised globally through Ariana Grande's portrayal in the two-part film. Allie Trimm as Glinda at the curtain call for her first show as a principal cast member in Wicked at the Gershwin Theater in New York City, on 4 March 2025 (Conor Clancy) That contract ended in March of this year, six months into the US-brokered ceasefire announced on 10 October 2025, and at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which drew headlines away from the wasteland that Gaza had become. It took nearly half a year before Trimm came forward publicly about the pressure she faced to stay silent on Palestinian rights while performing in one of the most lucrative and long-running musicals in the world. On 15 September, she posted a video on Instagram , emboldened by how rapper Macklemore handled his own firing from Ed Sheeran's tour by billionaire Robert Kraft . "While I worked at Wicked , I was told that there's an 'if' and a 'then'. If I keep talking about Palestine or Palestinian human rights on the internet, then I can expect the phones to stop ringing and all of the perks that should come with my contract to cease," Trimm said in her video. While the show's producer, Marc Platt, never had a one-on-one meeting with her, Trimm expressed concern with views he espoused on a podcast that include suggesting criticism of Israel is "Jew hate", and that actors in Hollywood who have called for a ceasefire in Gaza are "not completely informed". When the man at the top holds that position, the chilling effect trickles down to the company, Trimm told MEE. 'If I keep talking about Palestine or Palestinian human rights on the internet, then I can expect the phones to stop ringing' - Allie Trimm, Broadway performer "I started experiencing kind of pretty intense censorship," she said. "I reached out to the union for help when I was experiencing this. I also retained a lawyer. I was extremely distraught during the entire ordeal, and the union told me that I should double-check because the government has changed the definition of antisemitism, and I might very well be being antisemitic." The Trump administration has adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA) definition of antisemitism. Critics of the IHRA definition say it conflates antisemitism with anti-Zionism, including criticism of historic and current policies that led to the creation of the state of Israel in 1948 and the expulsion of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes. MEE repeatedly reached out to Actors Equity, the union representing 51,000 professional actors and stage managers, but did not hear back. Platt had most recently made headlines for reprimanding stage and screen star Rachel Zegler for posting "Free Palestine" on social media, which his son said hurt the box office returns for Platt's film, Snow White , in which she played the titular character. "I was singled out in this process" at Wicked , Trimm said in her video, which has garnered nearly 60,000 likes. "I was singled out, and I was the only employee that was subjected to this censorship and this monitoring." To look at how this industry has been impacted by the global fallout from Israel's ongoing assault on Gaza, MEE spoke with more than half a dozen performers, directors, and writers who have worked or continue to work in New York City's musical theatre scene, either on Broadway - meaning one of the 41 venues that seat at least 500 people in midtown - or Off-Broadway, including some regional theatres. 'The most Zionist of all' In June, 26-year-old Ali Louis Bourzgui won Broadway's highest honour - a Tony - for Best Performance by an Actor in a Featured Role in a Musical for the vampire rock musical The Lost Boys . It was by many accounts a major upset, given 80-year-old André De Shields was widely expected to get the trophy for his performance in Cats: The Jellicle Ball . "The people of Palestine," Bourzgui said in his speech , "deserve a free life, a full life, without occupation." The room responded with raucous applause. In this country's for-profit entertainment industry, it was a stratospheric shift. And that shift may have been inevitable with the changing demographic. "For Arab theatre makers and artists: May we continue to tell our stories and show our faces so our humanity becomes undeniable and our families can no longer be written off as merely collateral damage," Bourzgui, whose father is Moroccan, continued. "May they know the beauty of our kisses upon each cheek and the romance of a language rooted in passion for love and life itself." Ali Louis Bourzgui poses with the Best Performance by an Actor in a Featured Role in a Musical award for The Lost Boys at the Tony Awards on 7 June 2026 in New York City (Mike Coppola/Getty Images) The Tony Awards Instagram account typically posts videos of the speeches minutes after they take place. With Bourzgui, the clip was posted three days later, on 10 June, following an online outcry. "There was a lot of drama above the surface and under the surface in the theatre world about this speech, which clearly called for a free Palestine and end to the genocide," Nick Laparra , a social impact adviser for artists and the co-founder of Broadway Voices for Palestine , told MEE. The group had been holding a demonstration outside Radio City Music Hall, the venue for the awards in New York City, as they were handed out. CBS, owned by Paramount Skydance and pro-Israeli tycoon David Ellison , has the exclusive rights to broadcast the Tonys. "There was disagreement on whether the video should have been online, because it got taken down, and it was down for several days until the Tony Awards official account posted the entire clip, and then, and only then, did The Lost Boys , their official account, accept the collaboration on Instagram and post the full video." MEE reached out to Bourzgui's team for this story, but his publicist, Lisa Goldberg, said he would not be available for comment. Laparra called Broadway "the most Zionist of all the entertainment industries". "As soon as [performers are] posting about a 'Free Palestine', 'Stop the Blockade', 'All Eyes on Rafah', all these different ebbs and flows of the genocide over the last three years, there's been relentless pushback," he said. 'Most of everybody is pro-Palestine. They just can't speak up. They need this job. This is their dream job' - Nick Laparra, Broadway Voices for Palestine "Artists must pick a side," he added. "Palestine is the moral issue that separates." Laparra acknowledged that awareness and education on Palestinian rights have grown exponentially. "We have a lot of the biggest shows on Broadway represented in our group, and a lot of Off-Broadway, and a lot of the smaller shows," he said. Of the stagehands and performers he meets, he continued, "Most of everybody is pro-Palestine. They just can't speak up. They need this job. This is their dream job. So many [have] to navigate the complexities of this." "The problem... lies with the management. It lies with the investors." But "they can only do so much", which is why the tide is turning, one performer who is about to embark on a prominent role in one of next year's most highly anticipated shows on Broadway told MEE. The performer has chosen to withhold their name to speak more freely on the issue. "We're having conversations now that would have been a dream to have five years ago," they said. "I think people are existing too much in cognitive dissonance. I think the industry is reflective of what's happening in the country... it can only be defended by the media and by the levers of power for so long before people stop. We will continue to see progress as time goes on. Israel now has never been so unfavourable." Function Like any cultural institution, Broadway holds up a mirror to society. "Broadway reflects changes in the culture, and reflects political attitudes and changes in the city culture," Adam Feldman, a veteran theatre critic for TimeOut and president of the New York Drama Critics' Circle, explained to MEE. "One of the things that happened after the Covid shutdown was the Black Lives Matter movement became much more of a focal point for American discourse, and so in response to that, when the theatre came back, you did see a lot more plays... by black playwrights," he added. "That does, to some extent, push or reflect a political viewpoint." Two shows attempted to tackle Israel's wars and occupation this season: Giant , starring John Lithgow, which closed in June on Broadway; and Birthright , a play with a young ensemble cast that closed in August Off-Broadway. Giant largely centred on criticism of Israel falling into antisemitism. Birthright examined Zionism and landed on how no side is actually right. "Audiences don't like being lectured to," Feldman told MEE. "Yes, even when it's politics that they share, or maybe even especially when it's politics that they share, because it seems a bit redundant... one of the things that art does particularly well is set up space for exploration of complexity." The 2025-2026 season on Broadway saw 14.5 million attendees and brought in a whopping $1.91b while still operating at a loss , despite the ever-increasing cost of a night out at the theatre, and amid an affordability crisis in the US that is dominating the discussion ahead of the November midterm elections. The Broadway League, which is the trade association that represents producers and theatre-owners, has said a quarter of all ticket sales in the 2024-2025 season went to international tourists, many of whom will fly in just to see a show (or several). That's because the calibre, by all accounts, remains unmatched, though it is often challenged and inspired by productions staged in London's West End theatre district. The other outsized flashpoint in the lead-up to the midterms is arguably Israel , particularly among Democratic Party voters, where a deep divide has grown between the corporate pro-Israel establishment and the critical progressive wing, most vocally led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Democratic voters have traditionally made up the majority of those working in the liberal theatre space, and especially in the immovably blue New York City, where in addition to the Broadway scene and its adjacents, national touring productions will also rehearse in the city before taking off for sometimes years-long stints on the road. Forced far Off-Broadway What Palestinian artists argue is that they don't want to be spoken about when they could be doing the speaking instead - especially when the issue of Palestine has dominated the global political discourse for three years and created a fallout so profound that a US think tank developed an entire strategy on how to contain it . "Time and time again, we've seen these very clear examples of a blatant message that Palestine has no place in the theatre, and then, meanwhile, we're seeing amidst a genocide plays like Giant and Birthright being given massive platforms and selling out their runs without any backlash," Fouad Dakwar , a New York City-based Palestinian-American musical theatre artist, told MEE. He has created his own semi-autobiographical project, Fouad of Nazareth - a nod to his birthplace - which can next be seen at New York City's Festival of New Musicals later this month. The event is effectively an audition where new works could get picked up by commercial producers or non-profit outfits for further development. Palestinian-American artist Fouad Dakwar performs at the album release concert for his show 'Fouad of Nazareth' at Ars Nova in New York City, on 5 March 2026 (Valerie Terranova/Supplied) "I think what this all comes down to [is that] theatre in particular is such a gatekept art form," he added. "Broadway is a collection of theatres, and the people who own those Broadway theatres have the final say of what gets in the theatre." Dana Saleh Omar , a Palestinian-American performer based in Chicago, said getting to the hiring stage at all is the problem. "People that have been speaking out - you've noticed - none of them are Palestinian, and that's because they don't hire us in the first place," she told MEE. Palestine-centred projects have seen high-profile cancellations at popular Off-Broadway venues like the New York Theater Workshop (NYTW) and The Public Theater. In 2006, the NYTW scrapped My Name is Rachel Corrie , which was coming to the US from a run at London's Royal Court. When it later found a home at a different venue, The New York Times described it as a work " sympathetic to Palestinians ". Corrie, a 23-year-old US citizen, was killed in 2003 by an Israeli bulldozer in her attempt to protect a Palestinian home from demolition by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank. The Israeli military said its investigation concluded that her death was an accident. In 2016, the Public cancelled a planned run of Jenin Freedom Theatre's The Siege , about five Palestinian fighters who took refuge in the Church of the Nativity during the Second Intifada. The following year, it found a home elsewhere in the city, while a three-hour play called Oslo received rave reviews on Broadway. As its name suggests, it explores the backchannel dealings of the Norwegian diplomats who are credited with ultimately bringing together Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Palestinian Liberation Organisation chief Yasir Arafat to the White House to sign the Oslo Accords in 1993. While Rabin and Arafat are never seen in the show, the seemingly uncouth Palestinian negotiators, Ahmed Qurei and Hassan Asfour, were portrayed by Iranian actors. Oslo swept the Tony Awards in 2017. Then in 2018 came the musical The Band's Visit on Broadway, which also scooped up the most coveted trophies at the Tonys that year. It tells a story of an Egyptian military band that accidentally finds itself in the middle of a northern Israeli desert village, where a tender relationship develops between an Egyptian officer and an Israeli woman. The show does not address the occupation, but for Palestinians, the undercurrent is impossible to ignore. Omar was a standby on the show's national tour, which closed in 2022, after which she joined a regional production of the musical that was staged in Arkansas and Illinois between October 2023 and March 2024 - arguably at the height of Israel's assault on Gaza, and its simultaneous crackdown in the occupied West Bank, which has killed more than 1,100 Palestinians in the last three years. Palestinian-American performing artist Dana Saleh Omar stands outside The Public Theater in New York City, on 17 July 2026 (Mounira Elsamra/MEE) "It was very difficult," she told MEE earlier this year. "There is no Palestinian voice in that show, and especially when I was doing it in October of 2023, I felt that immensely... I kind of felt resentful of it because of that." Would she do the show again? "No, I wouldn't," she responded. In early 2024 , at a critical juncture in Israel's war on Gaza, Itamar Moses, the writer behind The Band's Visit, premiered his latest play, The Ally , at the Public, featuring visceral conversations about Zionism and including an outspoken Palestinian character. The New York Times review noted he "insisted he never tried to stack the deck to make sure one particular side of any argument seemed to win or lose definitively". Stuck Omar is now forging her own path by telling her own stories. "Art is something that I think can really speak to people in different ways and for different reasons, and that's why I love it so much... That's why you got to keep doing things that you want to see." In April 2025, Omar co-wrote and starred in her first short film, Stuck , in which a Palestinian woman wakes up dazed on the morning of 7 October 2023, entirely unaware of how much the world had just changed. 'We're so much more than our oppression. We're so much more than our trauma' - Dana Saleh Omar, Palestinian-American performing artist A younger version of the woman's father appears to her, in a bid to be a supportive presence, and perhaps impart lessons as she navigates the following hours. That character is more or less based on Omar's own father, Saleh Beshara Omar, who passed away in August 2025, she told MEE. "This project is in honour of him and his revolutionary spirit. I watched him be an activist my whole life," Omar said. "It's not our exact story. Stuck is kind of an amalgamation of a bunch of different Palestinian stories that I've picked up along the way, and this is like an alternate universe version of me that has never really used her voice until now." The short is at seven film festivals this year, and is showing this month alone at both the Toronto Palestine Film Festival and the Eastern Oregon Film Festival. "We're so much more than our oppression. We're so much more than our trauma. And if you don't give us chances to tell not just our sad stories, but our hopeful stories, our superhero stories, our everything... people can see that we're more than that," Omar said. The singular wholly Palestinian story that was showcased at a major venue since 2023 in New York City was the very traumatic A Knock on the Roof by Khawla Ibraheem, a one-woman play about a mother in Gaza who has rehearsed her life-saving run for every time a smaller bomb strikes the roof, warning of an incoming Israeli missile. It was part of the 2024-2025 lineup for the NYTW, which followed a more than 100-day HIV medication strike by one of the theatre's former resident playwrights who pleaded with the NYTW to call for a ceasefire in Gaza. It's unclear exactly how that highly publicised move impacted the venue's decision-making, if at all, but there was no publicly available statement calling for a ceasefire, and certainly not one that spells out the criteria listed by Theatre Workers for a Ceasefire , which now has 3,800 signatures from 80 organisations. "A lot of shows now are co-productions that need big-name stars attached, or big-name producers, and as a result, I think a lot of these theatres are terrified to do anything that rocks the boat, politically or otherwise," Dakwar, who has signed the pledge, told MEE. "If they were to lose one donor or one board member who gets them a substantial fund... Shows are just not able to be profitable with the current expenses." Mounting a show on Broadway in particular can run into the tens of millions of dollars before a single audience member has walked through the doors. This has led one of musical theatre's titans - and richest people - Andrew Lloyd Webber, to warn the costs are "unsustainable". 'We need so much more' MEE reached out to multiple Broadway producers as well as The Broadway League, and all declined to comment for this story. Diversifying the theatre space, much like Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion practices at the corporate level, has proven both innovative and lucrative, inviting a new audience to the box office. But in this political moment, meaningful change in hiring practices must go hand in hand with the normalisation of the discourse on Palestinian rights, an award-winning director of stage and screen, who spoke to MEE on condition of anonymity, explained. 'If you phrase it the opposite way, it’s technically illegal, right? Like to say, ‘I don’t want to work with someone because they are pro-Israel’' - Award-winning director The Palestine conversation "has been a source of connection" to find allies - sometimes more powerful ones - in the industry, the director, who explicitly identified as Jewish, said of the support groups that have formed around the subject. "For many of the actors that I spoke to, there was a job security question about what it meant to have these conversations... One of the things that we were excited about was showing actors that there are folks who do have hiring power, like myself, who have the same views that they do, and that they're not alone in those views in our community." The director pointed to an instance where they were interested in hiring a particular actor, and a producer texted them and said not to, because the actor in question is "antisemitic". "I said, 'What do you mean?' And then that producer referred me to a post that the actor had made, and the post was purely pro-Palestinian. And I then said, 'I don't think they're antisemitic. Let me explain'," the director recounted. The actor was ultimately not hired for other reasons, MEE was told. "If you phrase it the opposite way, it's technically illegal, right? Like to say, 'I don't want to work with someone because they are pro-Israel' could get me in trouble," the director added. While artists have to open doors for one another, a change in culture must also come from the top down, Clay Singer , who recently wrapped up a run in Masquerade Off-Broadway and Rhinoceros at American Repertory Theater in Massachusetts, told MEE. "Our mayor," he said, taking a moment to reflect on New York City's progressive kingmaker Mamdani, who has been a vocal critic of Israel and an advocate for Palestinian rights. "You watch the way that he speaks, and you watch the way that he navigates his power, and it's almost shocking because I don't think we have had a leader like this that we can look to as a light in a while, and I think... we can rally behind his voice." But Mamdani, like countless others voicing similar concerns, has been called an antisemite by Republicans and some Democrats, and the Israeli prime minister even made the point a key focus of his speech at the United Nations General Assembly last month. "As a Jewish person, I firmly believe condemning Netanyahu’s genocide on the Palestinian people has nothing to do with antisemitism," Singer said. "So much of Judaism is rooted in questioning, in seeking justice for the vulnerable and the suffering. It’s wrong to turn our eyes away from the violence Netanyahu has inflicted on the Palestinian people." On Wednesday, 10 days out from the one-year anniversary of the ceasefire, Israeli air strikes killed eight Palestinians in Gaza, among them women and children, as well as journalist Muhammad Abdel Aziz al-Najjar. According to the Palestinian Journalists' Syndicate, he is the 263rd journalist to be killed in the enclave. Speaking to MEE while taking her film on the road this week, Omar said the mounting toll on Palestinians on the ground made it uneasy to "celebrate the wins" when she has them. "It's not enough, you know? It's never enough for these innocent people that continue to be brutally murdered. We need so much more." Mounira Elsamra in New York contributed to this story . Around his home in Deir Nizam, northwest of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, the uprooted trees lay in a tangled heap of branches, stones and soil. Days earlier, Israeli bulldozers had arrived to raze land his family has owned since the 1960s. “What has this lemon tree done to them and their security?” Tamimi asked Middle East Eye, pointing to the broken branches. “I used to water this olive tree every day,” he added, pointing to another. Even if they destroy this house, I’m not leaving.” Tamimi’s case is part of a wider campaign targeting Palestinian agricultural land and olive groves across the occupied West Bank. In September, a series of military orders demanded the removal of vegetation and uprooting of trees across hundreds of dunams, just weeks before the olive harvest began. According to data from the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, 55 military orders targeting trees and vegetation were issued between the start of the year and September. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); They affected about 2,373 dunams, compared with 47 orders covering 1,613 dunams throughout the whole of 2025. On 20 September, following the killing of a settler in a shooting near Deir Nizam, the commission said a military order was issued targeting about 99.79 dunams of village land. The order required vegetation to be removed and olive and other trees to be uprooted. Four days later, another order targeted a further 94.79 dunams, giving landowners 12 hours to remove the trees themselves, according to the commission. Saleh Tamimi stands among olive trees uprooted by Israeli forces in his backyard, in Deir Nizam, northwest of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank (Mohammed Turkman/MEE) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Nathir Tamimi, another landowner in Deir Nizam, said his family owns about 24 dunams planted with olive trees. The trees, he said, had been inherited from previous generations. In recent days, Israeli forces had bulldozed about eight dunams of his land, along with neighbouring plots. He said about 140 dunams in the area had been cleared so far. Harvest under threat The escalation in tree-uprooting orders has affected more than Deir Nizam. On 24 September, Israeli forces bulldozed about 31 dunams of private land in Beit Rima, northwest of Ramallah, uprooting more than 400 olive trees. The operation came two days after a military order was issued requiring the removal of the trees. 'We refused to uproot trees we had planted with our own hands' – Afrah Sanaf, Beit Rima resident Hazem Rimawi, 61, said the trees uprooted from his three-dunam plot were heavy with fruit. “What happened in a few hours wiped out decades of work,” he told MEE. “I have no other source of livelihood besides this land and these olive trees. What use is the land now that the trees have been uprooted?” Afrah Sanaf, another resident affected by the bulldozing, said residents were informed on 22 September of a decision to remove trees in the area. They went to the municipality to examine the map, only to discover that their land was included in the order. Sanaf said his land was home to about 138 olive trees, many of them generations old and familiar to his family since childhood. He said he was 63 and could not remember a time when the trees did not exist. Afrah Sanaf, 63, with trees that had stood on his land for generations (Mohammed Turkman/MEE) The notice they received gave landowners 12 hours to remove the trees themselves. “Naturally, we refused to uproot trees we had planted with our own hands,” he said. According to Sanaf, the bulldozed land lies about three or four kilometres from the nearest Israeli settlement. ‘Rooted in this land’ On 25 September, Israeli bulldozers began uprooting olive and forest trees in Beit Ur al-Fuqa, southwest of Ramallah. The operation followed a notice targeting 29 dunams of Palestinian land planted with trees. The order was issued two days after a Palestinian carried out a car-ramming attack at an Israeli checkpoint near the village, injuring an Israeli soldier. Ali Samara, head of the village council, said the bulldozing had extended to about 60 dunams. He warned that continued operations could uproot at least 1,500 olive trees, some of them more than 200 years old. 'We are just like the olive trees we inherited: rooted in this land' – Nathir Tamimi, Deir Nizam resident In Kafr Malik, northeast of Ramallah, Israeli authorities issued a military order targeting more than 56 dunams, also calling for the removal of vegetation and olive trees. The escalation has come as farmers prepare for the olive harvest, which typically begins in October. For those whose fruit-bearing trees have been uprooted, the loss goes beyond this year’s harvest. The trees themselves can take years to become productive again. “What happened left us in a state of shock. It was an act of injustice,” said Sanaf. “The trees and land we lost were the source of livelihood we had relied on all our lives.” The destruction of terraces and topsoil, along with restrictions on access to farmland, threatens the land’s ability to be cultivated in the future. “The damage is not limited to the owners of the bulldozed land; it affects the entire town,” said Nathir. “The landscape has shifted from green olive groves to expanses stripped of their trees.” Nathir said he believed the uprooting was aimed at pushing landowners off their land. But he added that they remained determined to stay. “We are just like the olive trees we inherited: rooted in this land.” Occupation Fayha Shalash Ramallah, occupied Palestine News Post Date Override 0 Update Date Mon, 05/04/2020 - 21:19 Update Date Override 0

'The entire land is ours': Ben Gvir escalates calls for annexation of occupied West Bank Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 10/03/2026 - 10:19 National security minister says he would displace Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza if appointed defence minister Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir arrives at Tzur Yitzhak, central Israel, 7 June 2026 (Jack Guez/AFP) Off Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir claimed that the entire occupied West Bank “belongs to Israel” and has vowed to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and pursue the displacement of Palestinians if he becomes defence minister, Israeli media have reported . Speaking to Israel’s Channel 14, Ben Gvir said that, if appointed defence minister, he would work to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and push for Palestinians to leave the occupied West Bank and Gaza. The minister said that 60 percent of Palestinians want to “emigrate”. “I will dedicate time to this, and I will manage the process continuously. Every week, I will hold a discussion involving all relevant parties,” he said. “There is no difference between Areas A, B and C. The entire land is ours." Under the territorial framework established in the Oslo agreement between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation in 1995, Areas A and B were placed under varying degrees of Palestinian jurisdiction, while Israel retained control over Area C. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The United Nations regards the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as occupied Palestinian territory, stating that Israeli settlements in territory occupied since 1967 have “no legal validity”. Ben Gvir to release children’s book glorifying his racist ‘achievements’ in power Read More » The minister, who has repeatedly made genocidal statements against Palestinians, also called for fewer restrictions on Israeli soldiers’ use of force in the occupied territories. Asked how Israel could provide additional forces for operations in the West Bank and Gaza, he replied: “It is very simple: The more you allow soldiers to shoot and use force, the less manpower you need.” “I will remove the restrictions on our soldiers. Today, the police rules of engagement are much more lenient than those of the army,” he added. Ben Gvir also criticised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying the premier had “not want[ed] it enough” when it came to advancing a policy of Palestinian displacement. The remarks come weeks before Israel’s 27 October Knesset election, with Ben Gvir seeking to strengthen his position on the Israeli far right. Growing provocations Ben Gvir’s comments follow a series of Israeli incursions into Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem and Hebron during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot. On 29 September, some 966 Israeli settlers entered the Al-Aqsa Mosque courtyard in occupied East Jerusalem. Videos circulated by Israeli far-right groups showed participants conducting religious rituals, praying, singing and dancing inside the courtyard. Ben Gvir was among those who entered Al-Aqsa during the earlier incursions. Netanyahu tours tunnels beneath Al-Aqsa as Ben Gvir raids Jerusalem holy site Read More » The developments followed a visit by Netanyahu to tunnels beneath Al-Aqsa. The Israeli prime minister said during the visit: “It is moving to touch the rock of our existence. We are here very close to the Holy of Holies. We are here, and we will always remain here.” The status quo governing Al-Aqsa recognises the courtyard as an Islamic holy site administered by the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, although Israel controls security and access. Ben Gvir also visited the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron on 29 September alongside hundreds of Israeli settlers during Sukkot. “When I arrive at the Ibrahimi Mosque, I draw energy that makes me want to sing and rejoice,” he told Channel 14 during the visit. Israeli authorities had closed the mosque to Muslim worshippers during the Jewish holiday. The Palestinian Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs condemned the closure, calling it an assault on the mosque and on Muslim freedom of worship. The Ibrahimi Mosque has been divided between Muslim and Jewish worshippers since 1994, when an Israeli settler killed 29 Palestinian worshippers inside the mosque. 2 civilians martyred in firing by Indian forces near Kasur border: state media. State-run Radio Pakistan reported on Friday that two unarmed Pakistani civilians were martyred and another was injured in firing by India’s Border Security Force (BSF) near the border in Kasur. Citing security sources, the report said that three residents of Ladhar village went a few steps ahead of a border pillar when the BSF “opened fire on them without warning”. “The sources said two civilians were martyred while another sustained injuries in the firing. All three individuals were unarmed,” the report said. It identified the deceased as Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jutt, both residents of Jattan Wali Haveli, Ladhar. “The security sources further said that none of the three individuals had attempted to cross the border fence. They said the incident constitutes a violation of the border agreement and the standard operating procedures governing the Pakistan-India international border,” the report added. “Indian media, while continuing its tradition of a false-flag narrative, labelled the innocent civilians as alleged infiltrators,” the report said. The development comes a day after Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry lampooned India’s claims of “neutralising” a “terrorist” allegedly linked to the Pakistani military, presenting the individual during a press conference. Asked whether the recent allegations could trigger another armed conflict between the neighbours during the press briefing, he affirmed that Pakistan’s armed forces were always ready for any such move and warned of “very harsh” retribution.
