Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs392.76 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs399.64 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable from Oct 3 (Saturday) to Oct 5 (Monday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Sept 29 appreciated the success of the scheme , saying that it reflected a “whole of government” approach. Chairing a meeting of the National Steering Committee on Fuel Subsidy to review the implementation of the scheme, the deputy premier noted that the information, IT and petroleum ministries, as well as the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra), the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and all provinces, had made “concerted” efforts for the scheme. It was noted that to date, around 7.60 million registrations have been successfully made, and the token redemption process has entered the second week. Moreover, 7.71m tokens have been redeemed. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Doctors cannot run drug stores without licence: FCC. • Observes Pharmacy Act and Drugs Act perform different legal functions • Sets aside 2023 PHC order restraining regulatory action ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Friday ruled that a registered medical practitioner (doctor) may prescribe and dispense medicine to his own patient within the scope of Section 31(4)(a) of the Pharmacy Act 1967, but cannot maintain a medical store or retail drug outlet without a licence under the Drugs Act 1976. The FCC issued the ruling while setting aside a June 5, 2023 order of the Peshawar High Court’s D.I. Khan bench, which had restrained regulatory action against registered medical practitioners allegedly running medical stores and dispensaries. The FCC ruled that registration as a doctor does not exempt them from the licensing requirements of the Drugs Act. A two-judge FCC bench, headed by FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan and comprising Justice Ali Baqar Najafi, issued the verdict while taking up an appeal moved by the secretary of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa health department. The controversy arose when respondents, including Dr Muhammad Rizwan Rajpoot, who were registered medical practitioners, were found maintaining dispensaries/medical stores within their respective clinical establishments and allegedly stocking and vending pharmaceutical drugs without possessing the requisite drug sale licences. This culminated in an inspection conducted on Jan 21, 2020, during which the drugs were taken into custody through Form-6 and consequential show-cause notices were issued. The respondents invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of the PHC, challenging the legality of the regulatory action. Their writ petition was allowed by the high court through its impugned judgement of June 5, 2023. While setting aside the PHC order, Chief Justice Aminuddin observed that registration with the medical regulatory body and registration under the Pharmacy Act perform different juridical functions. Holding them otherwise would amount to judicially engrafting upon the licensing regime, an exemption which the rule-making authority itself had not enacted, said the nine-page judgement authored by the FCC chief justice. During the hearing, the FCC framed three core questions: whether the drug inspector had lawful authority to inspect and take action under the Drugs Act; whether registration as medical practitioners, coupled with Section 31(4)(a) of the Pharmacy Act 1967, gave them an unfettered right to stock and sell drugs without a licence; and whether the high court was justified in intervening at the show-cause stage. On the first question, the court held that Sections 17 and 18 of the Drugs Act empower inspectors to inspect premises, take samples, and search and seize drugs. Section 19 prescribes the procedure, including issuance of a receipt in Form-6. The FCC noted that no case had been established that the inspector concerned lacked appointment, territorial competence or authorisation. Drawing a distinction between the Pharmacy Act and the Drugs Act, the judgement observed that Section 31(4)(a) of the Pharmacy Act merely creates an exception allowing a registered medical practitioner to dispense medicine to his own patients or serve his own prescriptions. It does not authorise him to establish or maintain a medical store or retail drug outlet without a licence under the Drugs Act. “The legal effect of an exception cannot be enlarged beyond the prohibition from which it operates,” the judgement explained, adding that Section 23(1)(c) of the Drugs Act clearly provides that no person shall sell any drug except under a licence, and the expression “no person” admits of no occupational exception for registered doctors. The FCC emphasised that the Pharmacy Act was primarily concerned with regulation of the profession and practice of pharmacy, constitution of pharmacy councils and registration of pharmacists. Section 31(1) prohibits practice as a pharmacist by an unregistered person. Subsection (4)(a), upon which the respondents rested their entire claim, merely carves out an exception from that prohibition in favour of a registered medical practitioner who dispenses medicine to his own patients or serves his own prescriptions. Whereas the objective of the Drugs Act was to regulate the import, export, manufacture, storage, distribution and sale of drugs, Section 23(1)(c) employs language of unmistakable amplitude by providing that no person shall sell any drug except under, and in accordance with, the conditions of a licence issued under the Act. The expression “no person” admits of no occupational exception merely on account of the seller being a registered medical practitioner. The judgement pointed to the specialised mechanism under the Drugs Act, including the Provincial Quality Control Board and the Drug Court, which should examine technical and factual questions before judicial review. It clarified that Section 11 of the Drugs Act is not a conventional appellate remedy but part of the statutory machinery. The FCC also disapproved the argument that Article 18 of the Constitution protects the respondents from licensing requirements, stating that the right to enter a profession or trade was expressly subject to qualifications prescribed by law, and regulation through a licensing system was constitutionally permissible, especially for pharmaceuticals linked to public health. “Constitutional jurisdiction is essentially corrective and supervisory; it is not ordinarily a substitute for a fact-finding forum specially constituted under statute,” it observed. The FCC regretted that constitutional jurisdiction in the present case was exercised prematurely and upon an erroneous construction of the governing enactments. “The petition, therefore, merits conversion into an appeal and acceptance, with the result that the impugned judgement is liable to be set aside and the parties relegated to the statutory process for determination of the show-cause proceedings in accordance with law,” the court ruled. Some institutions have become hurdles to performance: Naqvi. LAHORE: The country’s system is in need of a reset, as some departments and institutions have become hurdles to ‘performance’, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Friday. The security czar, who had whipped up a political storm when he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country a few months ago, urged the business community to support the government’s efforts in this regard. Mr Naqvi made the remarks while speaking to businessmen in Lahore – reminiscent of his original tirade at the Pakistan Economic Summit in July. “As far as federal institutions are concerned, we do receive your complaints from time to time. It seems that some departments and institutions have become hurdles in the way of our performance. So whenever possible, we try our best to correct the things,” the minister said. Revives earlier call for ‘system reset’, seeks support from business community “I will not speak more on this and I don’t want to go into detail, as there are many things and we achieved many of them. But at this time, this country’s system needs to be reset, and we cannot do that until we have your support,” he reiterated. He hoped that whenever the system is reset, things will much improve. The interior minister, who has recently made several whirlwind trips to Iran as part of the country’s efforts to find a diplomatic solution to the ongoing hostilities between Iran and the US, also spoke at length about the neighbouring country’s progress despite decades of sanctions. In his words, those who hadn’t been to Iran thought of it as a war-torn country, with destruction everywhere. “The people who visited Iran with me returned astonished after seeing the scale of development in a country that has been suffering under sanctions for many years,” he said. “You name anything – their auto industry is manufacturing everything locally. I agree that export-led growth is necessary for this the country’s [economic uplift], but at the same time, we need to reduce our imports through local manufacturing,” he said, requesting the business community to come up with proposals related to both exports and imports. He stressed the need to learn from Iran’s economic development. “If they can do this despite sanctions for 30-40 years, we can do much more than them. And it is easy for us,” he maintained. PTI to begin march from south KP tomorrow. PESHAWAR: PTI Khyber Pakh­tun­khwa Secretary Information Shaukat Yousafzai said on Friday that the party’s protest march would start from the southern districts and be led by Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. “The march on October 4 will take place at any cost,” he said in a statement issued here. He said the procession from the southern districts would be led by the chief minister, while the procession from Malakand Division would be led by PTI provincial president and MNA Junaid Akbar Khan. He said processions from the southern districts, Peshawar, Malakand and Hazara would converge in Swabi, adding that preparations for the march had been completed and a shortage of resources would not be a hindrance. Shaukat Yousafzai says CM Afridi will lead procession Mr Yousafzai said the success of the government-opposition negotiations would depend on the government’s attitude. He said the PTI had been demanding access to incarcerated party founder Imran Khan, his transfer to a hospital and early hearings of his cases. He described PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan as a mature and conciliatory person who would find a way forward. “So far, I can call the government-opposition negotiations encouraging,” he said. He said both sides had presented their respective positions during Friday’s negotiations, adding, “Let’s see what happens next.” He further said the final destination of the protest march was Islamabad. “Governor’s rule is not the solution to the problems; it will make the situation even more serious,” he said. He said suggestions for imposing governor’s rule or an emergency were being made by non-political people in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If the government wanted to improve the situation, he added, it should immediately allow a meeting with Imran Khan. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

Govts should be allowed to complete their terms: CM Maryam. LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has said governments that perform well should be allowed to complete their five-year terms, arguing that the lack of policy continuity in Pakistan remains a major hurdle to development. She was addressing a delegation of the National Command Authority Senior Officers Leadership Course on Thursday, according to an official handout. Speaking on the occasion, she said Pakistan’s “excellent image and new face” had emerged before the world during the recent conflict with India, adding that the army and other security institutions were rendering invaluable services for the country’s defence. The chief minister said good governance and performance were essential to tackling internal security threats. “We are Pakistanis first, regardless of whether we belong to Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan or Gilgit,” she said, stressing the need for continuity in national policies. Credits PML-N’s extended rule over Punjab for ensuring policy continuity, leading to better governance; Azma says policies should not be sacrificed to ‘political changes’ Building on her argument for political continuity, CM Maryam said governance standards had improved because the PML-N had remained in government in the province for longer periods. She also claimed that terrorism had been brought under control in Punjab, but acknowledged that the threat had not disappeared, adding that the provincial government remained prepared for any possible attacks. The chief minister said the province previously had around 70 areas regarded as “no-go areas”, but claimed that there was no such area now. “I am responsible for the safety of 140 million people, so I had to take decisions that had not been taken before,” she said. Referring to criticism of her government, CM Maryam said there were occasions when she had to choose between “protecting myself or protecting the people”, adding that she had always prioritised the public. The chief minister said she had no personal grievances against anyone, and did not seek credit for herself. “I ensure 100 per cent merit in Punjab, and neither accept recommendations nor do people now approach me with recommendations,” she said. Listing her administration’s ‘achievements’, she said the government had strengthened security infrastructure, particularly in border areas, by establishing fortified posts and providing weapons and night-vision cameras. She also highlighted round-the-clock surveillance to detect terrorist activity. The chief minister said the Punjab government had established separate groups for administration and law and order and that special attention was being given to crimes against women and children. She said the government had dismissed around 1,000 police and revenue officials as part of measures against corruption and claimed that sustained action had created a fear of the law among officials demanding or accepting bribes. The chief minister said the government had established virtual police stations for women unable to visit police stations, particularly victims of domestic violence, claiming that hundreds of thousands of cases had been dealt with through the system. In a subsequent statement, Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari also stressed the importance of policy continuity, saying that CM Maryam’s “clear stance is that governments may change, but the national vision and policies aimed at public welfare should not change”. She insisted that the country’s development was not the responsibility of any single province, government or political party; rather, it is a shared responsibility of all. “Policies formulated for the country’s development and public welfare should not be sacrificed to political changes.” Ms Bokhari said that if a policy introduced today is abandoned or changed tomorrow merely because of a political change, the country cannot move forward. “Pakistan needs a consistent national vision and continuity of policies instead of short-term political agendas,” she noted. Capital blockade chokes Karachi Port operations. KARACHI: Pakistan’s effort to keep supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan out of the capital has led to a pileup of shipping containers in the nation’s main port of Karachi, 1,400 kilometres away. Truckers are refusing to drive north, for fear their vehicles will be seized and the containers used to barricade Islamabad ahead of an Oct 4 march on the city planned by Imran’s Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) opposition party. “Right now, going toward Punjab is like committing suicide,” said driver Javid ur Rehman, 35, who has halted such journeys, referring to Pakistan’s most populous province. “The police seize the vehicles and snatch the containers, and then we are left distressed.” Containers pile up as truckers halt northbound trips ahead of PTI march Steel shipping containers, packed with sand and welded together, have lined the roads into Islamabad for weeks, in preparation against a march, postponed from Sept 27, to demand Khan’s release from prison. The former prime minister was jailed in 2023 after being ousted by parliament. All convictions but one have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. His party remains under state scrutiny that has suppressed participation in recent protests, however, “This is not the way to stop protests,” said Rana Mohammad Aslam, president of the Karachi Goods Carrier Association. Authorities began stopping vehicles around Sept 5, weeks before the original march date, he said. Pakistan’s home, information, commerce and finance ministries did not respond to requests for comment. Punjab police and the provincial home department also did not respond. The containers are positioned ready for placement at key entry points into Islamabad, a capital region larger than the southeast Asian city state of Singapore. Transporters battling rising prices say they cannot afford to have trucks seized. Police requisitioned more than 2,000 vehicles in September ahead of the march, they added, many still loaded with cargo and held for days with little or no compensation. Their reluctance is leaving containers piling up at Pakistan’s main trade gateway, Karachi. The disruption was affecting routes to Islamabad, the military city of Rawalpindi, and the cities of Jhelum, Peshawar and Attock, Aslam said. Some operators had halted journeys beyond Gujranwala in Punjab, while others took alternative routes. Transporters mounting bills The bills are mounting for those whose containers have been seized, as daily demurrage charges on one such container alone can run into Rs30,000 to Rs40,000 ($110 to $150), Aslam said, adding to losses from missed deliveries and idle trucks. Consumer prices rose 10.26pc in September from a year earlier, while the transport price index climbed 27.43pc, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday. Operators are struggling to pay drivers and maintain their fleets, as international shippers still expect payment regardless of the reason for the delay, Aslam said. He said he was holding talks to find a solution, but transporters could stage their own protest if complaints go unanswered. For Pervaiz Khan, 50, the risk was enough to keep a load of chemicals parked in Karachi. “Right now, my vehicle is loaded, but I am not going,” said the father of five, adding that he had loaded his cargo of chemicals by night. “We depart from Sindh, and the moment we enter Punjab, that’s when our troubles begin.” Drivers stranded near Islamabad regretted lost days of work or earnings. “If the roads open, our children’s livelihoods will open up,” said Sagheer Ahmed, 51, who added that his children, awaiting him at home, relied on his earnings. “If not, we will just keep standing.” Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

EU agrees to release diesel stocks after US pressure. BRUSSELS: European countries agreed to release diesel stocks on Friday after the White House pressured governments to do so, in a bid to cool surging fuel prices linked to the Iran war. “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked diesel oil. The process will begin immediately,” President Donald Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. Trump’s statement followed talks on Friday among EU governments, who discussed a proposal by France for European countries to release 50 million barrels of diesel, and for International Energy Agency members to release 50m barrels of crude oil, according to sources. Under the proposal discussed by European governments, Europe would release part of the diesel volumes in a 20-day period, responding to Trump’s demand for a rapid release of fuel stocks. French President Emmanuel Macron chaired a videoconference with G7 leaders on Friday afternoon to discuss the energy situation, the Elysee Palace said. It was not immediately clear if G7 countries had agreed to France’s proposal on the volumes of fuel to be released. US diesel futures extended their price losses after reports of the stock release discussions, and were down more than four per cent to $4.4491 a gallon. Benchmark European diesel futures fell by over $100 a metric ton. The discussions underscore growing pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential ban on US diesel exports to help lower domestic fuel prices ahead of Nov 3 midterm elections. In weighing its response, the EU needs to balance the need to ease soaring fuel costs against preserving emergency reserves to safeguard against uncertain supply from Gulf producers due to disruptions caused by the Iran war. French President Macron spoke with Trump overnight, emphasising the need to work together to combat rising fuel prices and ensure the global availability of refined products, the Elysee Palace said. France currently holds the G7 presidency. US pressure on Europe According to sources, the Trump administration had told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories or face a potential US diesel export ban. The US had demanded that large European countries release 100m barrels of diesel within a 20-day window, the sources said. Global diesel supply has been hit by the Iran war and a Russian ban on exports after Ukraine damaged many of its refineries. Chinese refiners have also suspended fuel exports to bolster domestic stocks. The proposed 50-million-barrel release equates to approximately 17pc of the EU’s total emergency stocks of diesel and gasoil, Eurostat data showed. It reflects around 3pc of the bloc’s annual consumption of the fuel. Europe used to rely on Russian and Middle Eastern diesel imports, but has increasingly relied on imports from the United States in recent years. “Having been caught dragging their feet on promised strategic stock releases earlier this year and now jarred by possible US export restrictions, European countries will likely release more diesel and possibly crude from their stocks,” said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group. “European strategic stock releases are a necessary, if not sufficient, condition to prevent US export restrictions, which would still remain on the table given acute political anxiety in the White House about high pump prices.” Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

Five shop owners move court to include terrorism, murder charges in Gul Plaza fire case. KARACHI: A judicial magistrate on Friday issued notices for Saturday (today) to members of Gul Plaza Management Committee and the investigating officer (IO) on a petition filed by five shop owners of the mall, seeking to record their statements before the court to include charges of murder and terrorism. Speaking to Dawn , prosecutor Hassan Bhatti said that two applications had been moved by the shop owners before Judicial Magistrate (South) Aasim Aslam. He said the shop owners had already recorded their statements before the IO under Section 161 (examination of witnesses by police) of the criminal procedure code and now they wanted to record their statement before the magistrate. He further stated that the prosecution did not oppose the plea seeking to record their statements before the court. However, he added that the prosecution opposed the plea seeking to include charges of murder and terrorism and treat the incident as the Baldia Factory fire incident. Prosecutor Bhatti told Dawn that he argued before the court that the Gul Plaza fire was a separate incident. He added that in the Baldia Factory fire case, a chemical report had found phosphorus, and there was also an alleged intention behind the incident as the factory owners had not paid the ransom demanded by the accused persons. He added that the Gul Plaza incident was separate and that the fire had broken out unintentionally, as per statements recorded by prosecution witnesses. According to witnesses, he added that a teenage boy was playing with matchsticks, which led to the fire in the mall. Meanwhile, defence counsel Shaikh Jawaid Mir, representing members of the Gul Plaza Management Committee — Tanveer Pasta, Amar Ismail, Muhammad Ramazan and Muhammad Ameen — as well as the owner of an artificial flower shop, Naimatullah, and his over 11-year-old son, Huzaifa, had raised objections to the plea seeking to include murder and terrorism charges in the case. After hearing arguments from all sides, the court issued notices to the suspects and the IO regarding recording of their statements and directed them to appear in person on Saturday (today) for hearing. Regarding the plea seeking to include murder and terrorism charges in the case, the court adjourned the matter until Oct 7. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

‘PUBG-linked’ bank robber arrested from home in Lahore. LAHORE: The police claim to have arrested a young man hours after he looted Rs700,000 by getting a “bank robbery task” from the PUBG game at Bhatta Chowk in Defence here on Friday. DIG Operations Faisal Kamran told mediapersons that the robbery took place at around 9:30am near Bhatta Chowk. He said a masked suspect entered the bank premises after taking the guard hostage. He then reached the cash counter, along with the hostage guard, collected cash and escaped the scene. The crime was committed within a few minutes. The DIG said that soon after looting the cash, the suspect drove back to his home which showed that he was not a habitual criminal. DIG says financial difficulties pushed UK-returned youth to commit crime by seeking help from the online game He said police teams were formed soon after receiving an emergency 15 call about the robbery, adding that the police traced him through the Safe City and private cameras and reached his house, located a few minutes’ drive away from the bank. The DIG said that the suspect was identified as Subhan, who had returned to Pakistan from the UK on Sept 16. He said the suspect was living alone in Lahore as his family was settled in the UK. He said that the suspect had been playing the PUBG game for the last many years. On the day of the incident, he got a ‘task’ from the game to rob a bank and acquired a mask and a pistol from somewhere to execute the crime. He said the police interrogated the suspect when he talked about the game, keeping in view such incidents in the past involving young men. He said that the arrested suspect also briefed the police about the methods described in the game to carry out a bank robbery. The DIG said that the suspect was planning to flee to Islamabad with the looted money when the police raided the house. He said the weapon, looted cash and a briefcase were recovered from him. He said that the suspect had changed his vehicle’s number plates to mislead the police. The DIG said the suspect had £1,200 when he reached Pakistan, however, he spent the entire amount and had been demanding more money from his family. When his family refused, he planned the bank robbery to overcome his financial constraints, he added. He said that according to initial investigations, he was influenced by online gaming and web series. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

Rizwan, NCCIA tight-lipped after player appears for questioning. LAHORE: Pakistan’s wicket-keeper/batter Mohammad Rizwan appeared before the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) here on Friday in a case concerning allegations of online betting, gambling and leaking of team information from the dressing room during the Test series in England earlier this year. Neither Rizwan nor any NCCIA official were ready to respond to media queries after the cricketer came out of the agency’s office after more than three and a half hours of investigation conducted by four NCCIA officials. Rizwan, 34, was served a notice by the NCCIA under the Criminal Procedure Code Section 160. When asked how the conduct of the agency’s official was and what questions he faced, a smiling Rizwan said: “I am deaf (in this connection), the conduct (of NCCIA officials) was good. I am feeling hungry; so let me go” before leaving the venue. It may be mentioned here that the NCCIA had confiscated Rizwan’s mobile phone in England on Aug 30, reportedly, having some secret information. The agency had promised that it will return the phone in three hours but it was not given to the player before he was summoned for inquiry on Friday. It is still not clear if the NCCIA has returned Rizwan’s phone. And there is no information if the agency will again summon the player. It is learnt Rizwan was summoned for his face recognition, which is necessary for daily forensics of the phone. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

Car crashes into crowd in Australia, 10 injured. A driver lost control and crashed his car into a crowd of rugby league fans in the eastern Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday, injuring 10 people including children, police said. Thousands of supporters had gathered to farewell local rugby league side the Newcastle Knights ahead of their grand final match against the Sydney Roosters on Sunday. But the festive environment was shattered when an 18-year-old rugby fan “driving erratically” lost control of his vehicle and crashed into the crowd, police said. “He was revving the car, he was excited, he was a supporter, he was there for the joy of the moment,” Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris told national broadcaster ABC. “Somehow he lost control of the car… and he’s gone into the crowd.” Two people were in a critical condition — a five-year-old girl and 67-year-old man. Two other young children were hurt, police said. The driver had been taken into custody. “One person made a decision in a split second that put everyone at risk,” said Jenny Aitchison, the roads minister for the state of New South Wales. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said “my thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle”. “Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans,” he wrote in a post on X. And Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said on Instagram: “We’re thinking of you, your families and everyone in our Newcastle community.” “Sending our love and support.”

Indus Waters Treaty abeyance puts millions at risk, UNHRC event warns. UNITED NATIONS: India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance has raised concerns over the water security, agriculture and livelihoods of millions of people dependent on the Indus Basin, as the six-decade-old agreement faces one of its most serious challenges. The concerns were discussed on Friday, Oct 2, at a side event held in Geneva on the margins of the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council. The Council’s current session is being held from Sept 7 to Oct 7. The event, titled “Water Justice and Climate Resilience: Advancing Transboundary Cooperation in South Asia and the Middle East,” brought together legal experts, researchers, diplomats, practitioners and civil society representatives to discuss international water law, human rights, climate resilience, environmental justice and management of shared rivers. “Trans-boundary Water Challenges in South Asia” was among the principal themes, with particular attention to the Indus River system and the legal and institutional framework governing shared waters. The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), which administers the proceedings over the IWT, has determined that the treaty remains in force despite India’s decision to place it in abeyance. India has rejected the arbitration process, while Pakistan has cited the court’s order as supporting its position that the agreement remains effective. Rashida Abbas, founder of the Hydro-Justice Student Research & Policy Fellowship and a PhD candidate at the University of Geneva, addressed the South Asian dimension of the discussion, focusing particularly on the Indus system. Abbas said rivers should not be viewed solely as matters between states because their consequences are experienced directly by people and communities. “Rivers are not experienced only by states,” Abbas said. “They are experienced by people.” She linked water governance with human rights, noting that decisions concerning rivers can affect drinking water, agriculture, livelihoods, communities and health. Abbas argued that the future management of South Asia’s shared waters should be based on law, dialogue, science, functioning institutions and justice. She also stressed that trans-boundary agreements should not become optional when relations between states deteriorate. The discussion addressed concerns about using shared water resources as instruments of political pressure. Abbas highlighted the interests of downstream communities and the need for legal frameworks to protect their water security and human rights. Other speakers placed the Indus dispute within a broader discussion of trans-boundary water challenges. Majid Hawi Alwan addressed geopolitical pressures surrounding shared water systems in arid regions, including the Gulf and wider Middle East. His contribution focused on regional approaches in which water security is treated as a shared necessity rather than an instrument of unilateral leverage. Seraina Eldada brought a mediation and diplomacy perspective, examining the institutional design of transboundary water arrangements and the role of third-party mediation and permanent mechanisms in resolving disputes. Harmayn Mujahid, a legal scholar and fellowship coordination officer, linked water insecurity with human rights concerns. The discussion considered how changing river patterns and climate-related stress can affect vulnerable communities and why questions of equity need to be considered alongside state sovereignty in international water law. Tahir Mahmood addressed the relationship between resource scarcity and security, including risks associated with water-related tensions in regions already affected by political and territorial disputes. He also discussed prevention and resilience in the context of what he described as “hydro-terrorism.” The contributors noted that shared river systems face increasing pressure from climate change, population growth, environmental degradation and rising demand for freshwater. For Pakistan, the Indus Basin is particularly significant because its waters support agriculture, food production and millions of livelihoods. The river system has sustained human settlements in the region for thousands of years. The Geneva discussion placed the current India-Pakistan dispute within a wider question of whether institutions governing shared rivers can continue to function during periods of political tension. The PCA award represents a significant development in the legal proceedings, but it has not resolved the underlying political disagreement between India and Pakistan. The award and the separate order concerning interim measures, however, remain on the PCA’s official record. The Geneva meeting underscored the importance of maintaining established mechanisms for dialogue and dispute resolution as countries sharing vital water resources confront both political tensions and growing environmental pressures.

India-Pakistan blockbuster brings cricket fever to Japan baseball field. One of sport’s fiercest rivalries descended on a sleepy corner of Japan on Saturday as India and Pakistan clashed in the men’s cricket final at the Asian Games on a converted baseball field. The neighbours only meet in international tournaments because of long-running political tensions and matches between them typically attract television audiences of hundreds of millions back home. The gold-medal encounter in a suburban park in Nagoya was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for Indians and Pakistanis living in Japan. They lined up hours before the game to get into the cosy 2,500-capacity purpose-built Korogi Athletic Park Stadium. Pakistan’s Saim Ayub (L) celebrates as India’s Vaibhav Sooryavanshiis is caught out during the men’s cricket final match between Pakistan and India during the 2026 Asian Games at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin on October 3, 2026. — AFP “I think this is never going to happen again, India against Pakistan in Japan,” long-time Nagoya resident Umer Dar, draped in a Pakistan flag, told AFP . “I’m crazy about cricket but I never have the opportunity to watch it live because I’ve lived here for 26 years.” The last time India and Pakistan collided was at the T20 World Cup in February, where they played in front of a sell-out 35,000 crowd in Sri Lanka. The Asian Games setting was significantly more modest, with trees and a baseball pitcher’s mound just beyond the boundary. The atmosphere was as passionate as ever though, with fans waving flags and cheering every ball from the temporary stands. “We bought tickets three months back when they started selling them,” said Tokyo resident and India supporter Mohammed Kashim Raja. India’s Ishan Kishan (L) sweeps the ball during the men’s cricket final match between Pakistan and India during the 2026 Asian Games at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin on October 3, 2026. — AFP “At the time it was easy but it became really difficult for others to get them. “We heard that many people were selling them for high prices.” Cricket is a niche sport in Japan and neutrals at the final appeared to be virtually non-existent. ‘Always crazy’ There was more of a casual crowd at the bronze-medal match between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh earlier, on a warm and sunny day. Teachers Hiromi Niwa and Miki Kaede, both from nearby Gifu, said they knew nothing about cricket and had bought tickets out of curiosity. After reading a free leaflet explaining the rules and watching some of the action, Kaede said it had been a “really fun” experience. She was disappointed that their tickets did not get them into the final. “We didn’t realise that India against Pakistan was such a big deal until we actually searched for it,” she said. Pakistan players celebrate the dismissal of India’s Shreyas Iyer during the men’s cricket final match between Pakistan and India during the 2026 Asian Games at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin on October 3, 2026. — AFP Cricket has a growing presence in Japan and the sport got a huge boost when India played their first-ever T20 international against Japan last week. The historic match, celebrating 75 years of diplomatic relations, took place at Japan’s modest Sano International Cricket Ground outside Tokyo. It was Japan’s first T20 game against a full-member nation, and they gave India a huge fright before losing by two runs in a rain-shortened match. Kushal Gowda, an Indian fan living in Tokyo, said Japanese people were “trying to understand” cricket. “We were trying to explain to our colleagues in our office and they were curious and keen to know what it was about,” he said. Indian fans arrive for the men’s cricket final between Pakistan and India during the 2026 Asian Games at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin on October 3, 2026. — AFP “They kind of compared it with baseball.” The crowd for the Asian Games final was overwhelmingly supporting India, with only a few Pakistan flags and shirts dotted around the ground. A cheer went up when the gates opened to let fans in, and the party continued when the game began under clear skies. “Even if it’s in Japan, the craze of India versus Pakistan is always there,” said Tokyo-based India fan Afroz Khan. “Anywhere they play in the world, it’s always crazy.”

UAE investigators say flydubai co-pilot was planning 'terrorist act'. The UAE’s attorney general said the co-pilot of a flydubai flight to Israel had planned a “terrorist act” and used the cockpit’s emergency axe to attack the captain, the official UAE news agency WAM reported Saturday. The news agency quoted Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying that according to the initial findings of an investigation, “the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act” and had “attacked the captain in the cockpit with the emergency axe and tried to take control of the aircraft”. Barred from flying The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of a flydubai flight to Israel had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views, multiple media outlets reported. Scrutiny into the alleged assailant — who was identified in the reports as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami — and his motives has intensified after Wednesday’s drama aboard a Dubai-Tel Aviv route that officials say narrowly avoided catastrophe. During the flydubai flight, the jet’s Indian captain was assaulted by his co-pilot but he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that Omani authorities had banned the pilot from flying over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views, citing people familiar with the matter. CNN , citing two sources familiar with the matter, reported the pilot was removed from a job at Oman’s national airline last year over concerns about extremist views. Al Arabiya , citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views. The broadcaster said he had also spent time in Syria, raising concerns he may have been influenced by radical groups there. ABC News , citing senior intelligence and law enforcement officials familiar with the investigation, reported the suspect had allegedly been found in possession of extremist materials while he was a trainee.

Hasan Nawaz's fighting 96 against India in vain as Pakistan settle for Asian Games cricket silver. Hasan Nawaz’s fighting 96 went in vain as Pakistan fell 19 runs short of India’s 212-run target to settle for silver in the Asian Games men’s cricket final at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Japan on Saturday. Hasan struck five fours and seven sixes in his 51-ball innings before being caught behind off Shivam Dube from the final ball of the match, with Pakistan finishing on 192 for six. Needing 33 from the last over after reaching 179 for five, Pakistan kept their hopes alive when Hasan hit Dube for a boundary and then a six. But a yorker from the India all-rounder followed by two dot balls left Hasan needing four for his century from the final delivery. He attempted to clear the infield but was caught by wicket-keeper Sanju Samson, ending an innings that had briefly brought Pakistan back into contention. Hasan’s dismissal completed a remarkable recovery after Pakistan had been 39 for three after six overs. He and Saim Ayub put on 87 for the fourth wicket before Saim was dismissed for 29 off 22 balls in the 15th over. Hasan had reached his half-century from 28 balls and continued to attack India’s spinners, particularly Ravi Bishnoi, who conceded 44 from his three overs. Pakistan’s Saim Ayub (L) makes it to the crease to avoid a runout during the men’s cricket final match between Pakistan and India during the 2026 Asian Games at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin on October 3, 2026. Pakistan were 126 for three after 14 overs, requiring 86 from the last 36 balls, but Dube removed Saim and Abdul Samad in successive stages of the closing overs to keep India ahead. Saim was caught by Washington Sundar at square leg for 29 after attempting to use Dube’s pace, while Samad made nine before being caught by Tilak Varma off Washington in the 18th over. Despite those setbacks, Hasan continued the assault. He reached 68 from 36 balls after hitting Axar Patel for a six in the 16th over and then struck two fours in Dube’s next over, one of them coming through an edge after he flashed at a short, wide delivery. Pakistan reached 160 for four after 17 overs, needing 52 from the final 18 balls. India’s players celebrate the dismissal of Pakistan’s Abdul Samad during the men’s cricket final match between Pakistan and India during the 2026 Asian Games at the Korogi Athletic Park in Nisshin on October 3, 2026. — AFP Saad Masood kept the chase alive with two sixes in his unbeaten 12 off five balls, but Bumrah’s fourth over yielded only 11 runs, leaving Pakistan 33 short with six balls remaining. Dube was given the final over and conceded a boundary and a six to Hasan, but his yorkers at the crucial moment denied Pakistan the chance to complete the chase. India’s bowlers had earlier kept Pakistan under pressure after the batters had posted 211 for six. Pakistan’s chase had begun brightly enough but lost momentum after Sahibzada Farhan and Usman Khan departed in successive overs. Farhan made 10 off 11 balls before attempting a slog-sweep against Sundar and finding Patel at deep midwicket. Usman followed for three off six, slogging a fuller delivery from Patel to Dube at midwicket. Maaz Sadaqat, who made 23 off 18 balls with three fours, was then caught by Sundar off Patel at the start of the seventh over to leave Pakistan 39 for three. Hasan and Saim rebuilt the innings, taking Pakistan to 76 for three at the halfway stage. Hasan was then 26 off 18 and Ayub 12 off nine. The pair accelerated through the middle overs, with Hasan reaching his half-century from 28 balls. Their 87-run partnership gave Pakistan a realistic chance of chasing India’s imposing total, but Dube’s dismissal of Saim at 126 proved a significant turning point. Varma stars India had earlier been propelled to 211 for six by Varma and Dube, who added 62 from 31 balls for the sixth wicket. Varma remained unbeaten on 51 off 22 balls, striking three fours and four sixes, while Dube made 27 off 15 with two fours and two sixes. India had lost three wickets between the eighth and 15th overs after making an explosive start, but the late partnership lifted them beyond 200. Abhishek Sharma provided the initial impetus with 61 off 28 balls, hitting three fours and seven sixes. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made 15 off nine before being caught by Usman off Saim, while Sanju Samson was dismissed for two by Ahmed Daniyal. Shreyas Iyer made 21 off 24 balls and Ishan Kishan 20 off 18. Ishan fell to Arafat Minhas at 128, while Iyer was dismissed by Abrar Ahmed five runs later. India reached 114 in the first 10 overs before adding 97 in the second half of the innings. Varma reached his half-century from 21 balls and remained unbeaten, while Dube was dismissed by Daniyal in the first ball of the final over. For Pakistan, Arafat took two for 25 from three overs and Daniyal two for 43. Abrar took one for 29 and Saim one for 47. Saad and Sufyan Moqim went wicketless.

High school students in Paris' deprived suburbs spark national protest movement. Maisa, a 17-year-old in a poor Paris suburb who aspires to be an English teacher, joined tens of thousands of other students and their supporters this week in protests that spread across France over dilapidated schools, classroom overcrowding and teacher shortages. At Lycee Le Corbusier school in Aubervilliers, a suburb north of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis department, protesters said schools in poor neighborhoods like theirs faced the worst conditions. Last year I took the high school French exam without a French teacher, and teachers have a huge impact,“ Maisa said. French high school students block access to the Helene Boucher high school in Paris as part of a day of strikes and protests by public sector workers, including firefighters, in France, on September 29, 2026. — Reuters “These are not conditions to study in.” As protests raged at more than 1,200 French high schools this week, police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets in some cases. More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a “climate of unacceptable violence” and called for order. Amelia, 15, joined Maisa in the crowd outside the school gates and held a sign reading, “Our address should not decide our future”. She said she was demonstrating to demand the same rights as students elsewhere in the country. “The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It’s classist and racist,” she said. Ulysse Rabate, a political scientist at Paris 8 University, said the protests show the way that France’s marginalised urban neighbourhoods are increasingly influencing national politics. “When there is a collapse of the public service, of public education, those who feel it the most, and the most violently, are those at bottom,” he said. Political flashpoint The nationwide demonstrations and blockades, which began last week, have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for the government, which announced a series of deeply unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Thursday. The education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7 per cent to 65.53 billion, excluding teacher pensions. The education ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that education remained a priority and the below-inflation budget increase was due to population decline. The protests started in the Parisian suburbs, where poverty levels are high, then spread to Paris itself and other French towns, including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille. At Lycee Le Corbusier, classes including maths, humanities, English and sport have been cancelled since the start of the academic year due to a teacher shortage, according to Karima Kara Ali, an elected parent representative. In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of high schools took part in protests on Thursday, the CGT labour union said. Youth, teachers and parents in four towns complained of unsanitary school conditions and chronic staff shortages including of nurses and social workers. Louise Paternoster, a representative for the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the CGT’s education union, said the area does not get adequate resources for its student population and their educational needs. Two-thirds of schools in the department have unfilled teacher positions, according to a union survey. Not enough teachers “Our students are losing out on study time. Some schools don’t have drinking water. We are not equal to other departments,” she said, blaming shortages on government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions nationwide in 2026. In Pantin, a town on the northeastern edge of Paris, teacher Dilan Roche joined her students as they protested outside their school this week to support their demands and protect them from the police. Students stand near burning garbage bins amid clashes during a protest in Saint-Denis, near Paris. —Reuters “What they wrote on banners, we wrote in a letter to the local education authority: overcrowded classes, no nurses, no social workers which is problematic for students with learning difficulties, many living in precarity,” she said. While France ranks in the middle of OECD countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade, standing at 11,660 in 2024 and 11,910 in 2010, according to education ministry data. The last nationwide high school protest movement on this scale demanding more funding came in the 1990s. That followed the government sharply expanding access to the baccalaurat, the school-leaving exam that typically paves the way to university, without providing schools with sufficient additional resources, said Professor Clemence Cardon-Quint at Paul Valery University, who researches education funding. The movement won an increase in funding, but spending per student later stagnated despite growing demands on schools. Cardon-Quint said students and teachers have taken on additional responsibilities over the years, including navigating Parcoursup, the university admissions system introduced in 2018 and criticised by some students and teachers as opaque and discriminatory. “In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities,” said Cardon-Quint.

Pakistan summons Indian envoy over killing of 2 civilians by border troops. Pakistan summoned the Indian chargé d’affaires to lodge a strong protest over the killing of two Pakistani civilians by Indian Border Security Force (BSF) personnel in the Bedian sector along the international border, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Saturday. Two unarmed Pakistani civilians were martyred and another was injured in firing by India’s BSF near the border in Kasur on Friday. “The BSF personnel resorted to unprovoked and lethal force against unarmed civilians. Such use of force was wholly unjustified and grossly disproportionate, resulting in the tragic loss of two precious lives,” the FO said. Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterise the deceased as “infiltrators”, it added. The FO said the incident constituted a serious violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to life, and raised concerns over the protection of civilian life under international law. It called on the Indian side to “conduct an immediate, transparent and credible investigation”, take appropriate disciplinary and legal action against those responsible, and formally communicate the findings and action taken to the government of Pakistan. India was further urged to “respect fundamental human rights and international law, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures, exercise maximum restraint in such situations, and take effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future”, the FO said. The three civilians were residents of Ladhar village and had moved a few steps ahead of a border pillar when the BSF opened fire on them without warning. All three were unarmed. The deceased were identified as Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jutt, both residents of Jattan Wali Haveli, Ladhar. The injured civilian was taken for medical treatment. According to security sources, none of the three men had attempted to cross the border fence, with the incident described as a violation of the border agreement and standard operating procedures governing the international border. The development comes a day after Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry lampooned India’s claims of “neutralising” a “terrorist” allegedly linked to the Pakistani military, presenting the individual during a press conference. Asked whether the recent allegations could trigger another armed conflict between the neighbours during the press briefing, he affirmed that Pakistan’s armed forces were always ready for any such move and warned of “very harsh” retribution.

IWT’s future. TOGETHER with the Kashmir dispute, India’s unilateral suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty has become the biggest source of bilateral friction in the subcontinent. In a controversial move, New Delhi held the decades-old agreement ‘in abeyance’ in 2025 after the Pahalgam episode . But as Pakistan’s senior leadership has highlighted, Indian brinkmanship in this regard may set a negative precedent globally, while also planting the seeds of a new conflict in South Asia. Speaking at an event in Islamabad the other day, Information Minister Atta Tarar said that India’s unilateral action vis-à-vis the IWT could threaten global water governance . He termed New Delhi’s moves “morally bankrupt and devoid of ethics”. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had raised the issue earlier, when he addressed the UN General Assembly last week. He did not mince his words when he said that diverting Pakistan’s water would amount to an “act of war” . This is not mere rhetoric. The Indus and its tributaries are Pakistan’s lifeline, and the country cannot allow India to blackmail it using these precious waters. India has ruled out restoring the treaty until Pakistan acts against ‘cross-border terrorism’. This is a weak alibi being deployed to take what belongs to Pakistan. New Delhi has remained adamant despite the ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in August that the IWT could not be unilaterally suspended. India has brushed aside the court’s decision. Along with the key issue of water rights, the larger question is what sort of precedent India wants to set. Its leaders speak of multilateralism and the global ‘rules-based order’. Yet in practice, when they scupper bilateral treaties and refuse to recognise decisions by respected arbitrators, the Indians in fact promote the law of the jungle. Pakistan must continue to pursue its legitimate rights with regard to the Indus waters. It must also point out the double standards India adheres to — claiming to uphold global norms, yet trampling on international law. If the IWT dispute is left to fester, or worse, if India takes further steps to cut off Pakistan’s share of water, a new conflict in South Asia is quite possible. In order to avoid such a grim scenario, saner elements in India must work towards restoring the IWT, and addressing all other outstanding issues in a civilised manner. Published in Dawn, October 3rd, 2026

11 terrorists killed during operations in KP, Balochistan: state media. Security forces killed 11 terrorists during intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, state media reported on Saturday. State-run Radio Pakistan reported that five Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists had been killed during an IBO in KP’s South Waziristan district. Quoting security sources, the report said that security forces were continuing effective operations against Fitna al-Khawarij in KP under the Azm-i-Istehkam vision. The state uses the term Fitna-al-Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. “The security forces targeted and destroyed the hideouts of Fitna al Khawarij during the successful operation, killing five terrorists,” state media said, “A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was also recovered from the killed terrorists.” “The Fitna al Khawarij terrorists are suffering heavy losses in intelligence-based operations, being conducted in KP,” Radio Pakistan quoted the security sources as saying. “Security forces are committed to completely eliminate the menace of terrorism and ensure sustainable peace in the country under the Azm-i-Istehkam vision,” the security sources said. In a separate operation, PTV News reported that security forces killed six terrorists in the Gorander and Mashkel areas of Balochistan during an operation. “Security forces continue effective operations against Fitna al Hindustan under Operation Raddul Fitna 3,” the report said, quoting the security sources. State media, citing security sources, said that the terrorists belonging to Fitna al Hindustan attempted to flee after opening fire on a security checkpost in Mashkel. “Security forces responded promptly and killed the fleeing terrorists,” according to security sources. “Security forces remain determined under the Azm-i-Istehkam vision to completely eliminate the scourge of terrorism from across the country,” the security sources affirmed. KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time. The province, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August compared with 36 in July, representing an increase of 50 per cent, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). Since the call was made, the administration has the been gearing up to stop the protestors from entering Islamabad, with hundreds of containers being placed. Additional personnel have also been deployed from Sindh and Punjab police. The letter, available with Dawn , from the office of the chief commissioner requested that the “provision of 3,000 personnel of Pakistan Rangers with command structure to Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) Police may be extended from Oct 5 to 15, 2026”. An earlier notification issued by the interior ministry stated that the deployment had been authorised from Sept 20 to Oct 5. According to the previous notification, the deployment had been authorised under Sections 7(b) and 10 of the Pakistan Rangers Ordinance, 1959, and Sections 4 and 5 of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, to perform functions specified under the laws, as authorised by the Islamabad chief commissioner or the provincial government. “The deployed troops may respond appropriately in self-defence to any threats or violent activities encountered in the course of their duties as per rules/regulations in vogue,” the earlier notification stated. The interior ministry separately directed that in case of attacks by disruptive and armed groups, Rangers and police would take all appropriate and necessary counter-action in self-defence and take measures to deal with any violent activity. Meanwhile, gatherings in the federal capital are also banned under the Peaceful Assembly and Public Order Act 2024 , which had been rushed through the National Assembly amidst the opposition’s outcry. Asian Games: Pakistan hockey claim comeback bronze as volleyball end 64-year wait. Pakistan’s hockey team produced a brilliant come-from-behind victory to claim bronze at the Asian Games, beating South Korea 5-3 at the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium on Saturday, while the volleyball team ended a 64-year wait for a medal. The medal in hockey arrived a day after heartbreak against bitter rivals India, who edged Pakistan 4-3 in a dramatic semi-final to advance to the gold-medal match against Malaysia. Pakistan could not have started the bronze playoff better. Penalty corner specialist Sufyan Khan gave them the lead inside four minutes, converting from a set piece to make it 1-0. The lead did not last, though — Shakeel Moin picked up a yellow card in the seventh minute, and with Pakistan a man short, South Korea levelled through Gangsan Lee in the 12th minute. Korea then took control, with Yongbok Kim putting them ahead in the 18th minute before Jihun Yang doubled their advantage to make it 3-1 in the 25th. Pakistan pulled one back right on the stroke of half-time, Abdul Rehman converting a penalty corner to make it 3-2 and keep the contest alive. South Korea threatened to pull clear again early in the third quarter — Yang had an effort saved, and Lee spurned a clear chance — while at the other end Pakistan pushed for an equaliser without reward. Abu Mahmood saw a penalty-corner effort saved, Mohammad Ammad had a shot stopped by Korean goalkeeper Jaehyeon Kim, and Pakistan were unable to convert two further penalty corners before the quarter ended with them still trailing 3-2. Korea looked to be closing the match out early in the fourth quarter, with Yang twice going close from penalty corners, but Pakistan refused to fold. Rana Waheed levelled the match at 3-3 with a field goal in the 52nd minute, and with under seven minutes left on the clock, struck again from a penalty corner to put Pakistan ahead for the first time since the opening quarter. Hannan Shahid added gloss to the win with a further goal in the 59th minute, sealing a 5-3 victory and the bronze medal. The result marks a notable recovery for a team that last won Asian Games hockey gold in 2010 and silver in 2014, giving Pakistan something to build on after Friday’s narrow semi-final defeat to India. Bronze at last Earlier, Pakistan’s volleyball team capped their impressive Asian Games run with a bronze medal at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Gymnasium, beating China 3-0 to end a 64-year wait for a medal in the sport — their first since claiming bronze at the 1962 Jakarta Games, behind Japan and India. Members of Pakistan volleyball team celebrate after defeating China in the Asian Games bronze medal match at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Gymnasium in Okazaki, Japan, on October 3, 2026. —Courtesy POA The medal came a day after Pakistan’s hopes of reaching the gold-medal match were ended by Iran, the three-time defending champions, who beat them 3-0 in the semi-final. Iran will face host nation Japan in the gold-medal match. Pakistan, needing to beat China to secure the bronze, did so in straight sets: 25-18, 25-16, 25-18. Opposite hitter Murad Khan led the way with 18 points. Outside hitters Afaq Khan and Ali Usman Faryad added 14 apiece, with Musawer Khan contributing eight; Mohammad Hamad and Hamid Yazman also added three. China opened the first set with a block at the net and the sides traded evenly until 4-4, before China pulled ahead 7-4. Pakistan’s defence steadied the ship, levelling at 9-9, and the set stayed tight as the lead changed hands more than once; Pakistan briefly went ahead 11-10 before China hit back with two straight points to lead 12-11. From there, though, Pakistan took over. They built a two-point cushion at 16-14, stretched it to 19-15 as their spiking began to click, and kept improving their serve-receive as the set slipped away from China. Pakistan closed it out 25-18 in 21 minutes. The 26-year-old Murad top-scored in the set with six points, Ali Usman added four, and Afaq and Musawer chipped in three apiece. The second set followed a similar script early on — level at 4-4 before China again moved ahead 7-4 — but a timeout appeared to settle Pakistan’s nerves. They came back to level at 8-8, then took the lead for good at 10-9. From there the gap only grew: 16-11, then 19-13, then 23-15, with Pakistan’s attacking numbers doing the talking — their spikes were landing successfully 75 per cent of the time (33 of 44 attempts) compared to just 45 per cent for China (17 of 38), and Pakistan out-blocked China five to three at the net. Pakistan wrapped up the set 25-16 in 20 minutes. Murad and Afaq both scored six points in the set, while Musawer, Mohammad Hamad and Ali Usman added two each. Pakistan carried that momentum straight into the third, racing to a 6-1 lead before China briefly responded to close to 7-6. Pakistan pushed on regardless, building leads of 10-6, then holding off a China fightback that twice closed the gap to within a point or two, before pulling clear again at 15-12 and 18-14. The lead stretched to 22-17, and after that China could only manage a single further point as Pakistan closed out the set — and the match — 25-18 to confirm the bronze medal. The statistics told the same story as the previous two sets: Pakistan’s spike success rate was 69 per cent (15 of 22) to China’s 39 per cent (10 of 26), and Pakistan recorded six blocks in the set to China’s none. Ali Usman and Murad led the scoring in the decisive set with six points each; Afaq and Hamid Yazman scored four each, while Musawer and Hamad added two apiece. The result marks the finest Asian Games showing in Pakistani men’s volleyball history outside of that 1962 bronze, and comes on the back of a strong campaign that also included wins over Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and India before the semi-final defeat to Iran. Ethiopia's Tigray rebels abandon regional capital as govt advances. Tigray rebels were abandoning their regional capital in northern Ethiopia on Saturday, a local journalist and residents told AFP , as pro-government forces advanced on the city. Fighting erupted on September 23 in northern Ethiopia as the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks into neighbouring states, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020-2022 civil war. But federal forces and pro-government militias have pushed them back in recent days and they were heading north towards the regional capital, Mekelle. “TPLF militants and leaders are leaving Mekelle,” the journalist said, adding that federal forces had not yet been seen inside the city. He said government offices and police stations had been left without security personnel. “I am concerned that government and public property could be exposed to looting because there are no security forces in the city,” a local resident told AFP . “Lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life. I want us to quickly return to law and order,” added another resident. The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, and kicked out a government-appointed administration earlier this year. In a video message on Thursday, its leader Debretsion Gebremichael implied the TPLF would continue guerrilla-style attacks as they did when Mekelle fell to government forces in 2020 during the early stages of the last war. Their insurgent campaign ultimately led to the TPLF retaking the city in mid-2021. “We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose,” Debretsion said. Regional tensions The conflict has triggered a breakdown in Ethiopia’s relations with Eritrea and Egypt, who it accuses of supporting the rebels. Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara on Thursday, while Eritrea responded that it would “sever all diplomatic ties”. Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to its coastline. The TPLF’s Debretsion said in his video message that “the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea”. Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat without explanation, prompting a reciprocal move by Cairo. Counter-offensive The rebels initially made advances in neighbouring Afar and Amhara states, working alongside local militias. But they were pushed back this week, and the government launched a counter-offensive into Tigrayan territory along three axes towards Mekelle, according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank. There were reports that Mekelle’s airport, on the southern approach to the city, had fallen to a pro-government militia on Friday. But social media accounts are difficult to verify. Media access is heavily restricted and there have been significant communications blackouts. Earlier, a humanitarian source told AFP on condition of anonymity that the TPLF had been entirely pushed out of Afar. The TPLF ruled all of Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, when they were marginalised with the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region. The tensions led to a civil war from 2020 to 2022 — one of the deadliest in the world in recent times — that left more than 600,000 dead, according to the African Union. The Pretoria Peace Agreement of 2022, brokered by African institutions and Washington, maintained an uneasy calm until last year, but was never fully implemented.

Govt, opposition begin second round of talks ahead of PTI's Islamabad march. Delegations from the government and the PTI gathered for a second round of talks on Saturday afternoon to discuss various issues, including the latter’s planned Oct 4 march to Islamabad. Talking to Dawn , TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousufzai said comments made by PPP leader Sherry Rehman on Friday had triggered a controversy, leaving the situation unpleasant until late at night. “The opposition alliance held a meeting before the start of the talks, during which the government side’s views regarding the law and order situation in KP were discussed. After consultation with the KP chief minister, a response was prepared, which will be presented to the government side during the meeting today,” he said. Replying to a question, Akhunzada said it was also decided that it would be proposed during the meeting that no one would issue a media statement regarding the dialogue and that a joint statement would be issued after the meeting. He said the joint statement would reduce chances of confusion and differences of opinion. Afridi adamant on long march Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi remained adamant about holding the long march on October 4, vowing to prevent a repeat of the events of May 9. His remarks came as the government and the opposition are scheduled to hold the second round of talks today. In August, PTI announced a long march to Islamabad on September 27 against what it called the “illegal imprisonment” of the party founder and ex-prime minister Imran Khan. However, a couple of days before its scheduled long march, the party postponed the march till October 4. In a social media post on X, CM Afridi said PTI was the largest and most popular political party in Pakistan. “Pakistan is a democratic country whose Constitution grants us the right to peaceful protest.” On October 4, he said an “ocean of people” would begin its journey from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat at 1pm. The party would continue its struggle until the supremacy of the Constitution and the law was ensured in Pakistan and an independent judiciary was restored, CM Afridi added. “All demands of the PTI are in accordance with the constitution and the law.” In his post, he stressed that the party would “neither allow May 9 to happen again nor allow anyone else to repeat it”. Reacting to the KP CM’s remarks, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said his statements could affect the ongoing negotiation process even though the government wanted them to be “meaningful and fruitful”. He urged PTI leaders to refrain from making such statements until the final stage of the negotiations, so that the dialogue process was not “harmed”. “The language that Sohail Afridi is using against his opponents and our leadership does not seem like that of a chief minister; his statements are extremely indecent and reprehensible,” Chaudhry said. In a post on X a day earlier, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, an ally of the PML-N government, pressed PTI to unconditionally call off the long march, which, he said, would allow the country to come together to address the threat of terrorism and threats emanating from neighbouring countries. Bilawal also welcomed the government’s decision to work with his party and jointly engage with the opposition “to find political solutions to political problems”. On Friday, PTI Khyber Pakh­tun­khwa Secretary Information Shaukat Yousafzai said that the party’s protest march would start from the southern districts and be led by CM Afridi. “The march on October 4 will take place at any cost,” he said in a statement. Also on Friday, the army’s top brass warned that any attempt at creating agitation or a “May 9-like situation” would be dealt with “decisive force”. The warning came during the 277th Corps Commanders’ Conference in Rawalpindi, which was presided over by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. “[The] forum underscored the importance of internal stability and resolved that any attempt to cause agitation or create [a] May 9-like situation, on any pretext whatsoever, will be dealt with decisive force and rule of law, without hesitation and discrimination,” a statement from Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said. For the first time in almost three years, representatives of the federal government and the opposition PTI formally came together on Friday for talks aimed at easing the political tension in the country, and apprised each other of their positions. Though neither side shared its specific demands with the media, both were hopeful of a positive outcome from the meeting, which was chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq. Sources on both sides told Dawn that the PTI wants its incarcerated founder Imran Khan to be shifted from jail to a hospital for medical treatment, while the government has insisted that the opposition call off its protest march on Islamabad, scheduled for Oct 4. The government side included Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam, PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, along with the PPP’s Senator Sherry Rehman and MNAs Syed Naveed Qamar and Ejaz Hussain Jakhrani. The opposition delegation, led by Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, according to the Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), comprised PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Amir Dogar, former NA speaker Asad Qaiser and PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja. Emergency option The talks come as the PTI remains resolute on the march. Federal ministers have warned that the Centre would have no option but to impose governor’s rule or an emergency in KP, citing the province’s security situation and the protest call, while the PTI has warned of dire consequences if such a step is taken. The decision to hold talks was taken on Thursday at a presidency meeting attended by President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Mr Naqvi, Attorney General Mansoor Awan and other PPP and PML-N leaders. A source privy to the huddle told Dawn the emergency option was discussed, but participants agreed to first give the opposition a chance to settle matters peacefully through dialogue, and to seriously consider an emergency only if the PTI did not back down. The coalition also believes the march will remain confined to KP and not enter Punjab or Islamabad. On Thursday, Sanaullah said the government and PTI were engaged in “off-the-record talks” over the protest, and that the decision on the march rested with the PTI’s senior leadership, “with whom off-the-record consultation is ongoing”. “So let us see, even if they do not postpone it, we have arrangements in place to stop them,” he warned. Separately, the prime minister has invited Achakzai for dialogue, and the two are expected to meet in the coming days.
