They explore the mood at the UN, its shifting relations with Washington and its shrinking role in peacemaking worldwide, particularly in the Middle East. Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms pfranz Fri, 09/18/2026 - 21:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Somali police officers walk along a road median while patrolling a busy street in Mogadishu, on November 10, 2025. TONY KARUMBA / AFP Commentary / Africa 18 September 2026 16 minutes Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms The multilateral missions that have helped the Somali government fight Al-Shabaab for nearly two decades may be coming to an end. Mogadishu and its partners should get started now developing a plan for what they will do next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia The multilateral missions that have protected Somalia’s government from the jihadist insurgent group Al-Shabaab since 2007 could be drawing to a close. In early July, the U.S. informed the African Union (AU) that it would not back an extension of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) – which provides crucial logistical assistance to the AU’s Support and Stabilisation Mission – beyond the end of its current mandate in December. The U.S. position has subsequently softened, with U.S. diplomats telling the AU in September that Washington would consider a twelve-month extension before calling a stop to further UN aid. This development buys time for a more orderly drawdown or some kind of transition. But the reality remains inescapable: the security blanket that Somalia has lived under for almost two decades is on borrowed time. The forthcoming UN General Assembly provides a prime opportunity for the Somali government, the AU and its security partners to kickstart essential discussions about how to keep Somalia safe. Given the AU mission’s reliance on the UN to provide water, food, fuel and transport, it will almost certainly be unable to continue in anything like its present form without UN help. The AU, its foreign partners and the Somali federal government are considering how to keep the mission going, but they do not have any particularly enticing options in mind. There is no clear alternative to the UN office, whose budget is nearly half a billion dollars, when it comes to setting up, running and paying for a multinational force. That said, predictions that the prospective end of UN and possibly AU security assistance will see the government collapse and Al-Shabaab emerge victorious are wide of the mark. While Al-Shabaab remains a major threat to the Somali government and controls swathes of southern and central Somalia, the group is largely confined to rural areas. The government’s grip extends to most urban centres, with security in the capital Mogadishu improving sharply in recent years. Support from the UN has helped maintain this precarious status quo. But an end to multilateral assistance need not culminate in the federal state’s downfall, even if a mismanaged transition could spell trouble. A combination of Somali and other international forces, including those already stationed in the country, should form part of a new international security structure. It is now up to Mogadishu and its international partners to begin planning this shift before it is too late. Approximate areas of operation for AUSSOM troop contributors. Some troop contributors maintain bilateral contingents in addition to their AUSSOM deployments. Source: Crisis Group research as of September 2026. CRISIS GROUP More Trouble for a Struggling Mission The AU mission and its UN logistics support office – the mainstay of foreign assistance for Somalia’s security – rely on troops from Africa and funds from farther afield. Ugandan troops were the first to be deployed upon the mission’s launch in 2007, followed soon thereafter by forces from Burundi and Djibouti. Kenya and Ethiopia joined in 2012 and 2014, respectively, after first launching their own bilateral interventions to safeguard their borders from Al-Shabaab incursions. The mission pushed the jihadist group out of many urban centres in south-central Somalia in the 2010s, including Mogadishu in 2011. More recently, however, the AU has struggled to find money for the mission, with long-time donors like the EU whittling down their contributions and pushing for the exit door. The mission has been running a large deficit for several years, even as it has taken measures to cut spending. Troop numbers have dwindled from 22,000 in the mid-2010s to around 12,000 today. Instead of launching offensive operations deep in the hinterlands controlled by Al-Shabaab, the mission has turned more toward protecting urban areas it already holds, while playing a supporting role in Somali army campaigns. The financial crunch has since extended to the UN’s logistical support, funded through UN assessed contributions – mandatory dues paid by all member states to underwrite the global body’s operations. Even before the Trump administration took office, U.S. officials were wary of the model that sees UN finances flow to a non-UN mission, regarding it as an undesirable precedent. In early 2025, the U.S. blocked a proposal for the AU mission to also receive funding through UN assessed contributions, arguing in part that the UN is already spending heavily on UNSOS. In September 2025, the U.S. shelved planned contributions to the UN peacekeeping budget, including for UNSOS. Hence, its refusal to support the office’s existence any further does not come as a complete surprise. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Despite this apparent contradiction, the U.S. government believes that the status quo is no longer tenable: the multilateral missions are not as effective as they once were, while the Somali government should bear the primary responsibility for leading the fight with Al-Shabaab. U.S. diplomats believe that Somali elites are skirting their duties, preoccupied with pursuing political vendettas rather than combating jihadists. It is difficult to know if President Donald Trump’s evident personal animus toward Somalia has also played a role. A number of U.S. officials agree that ending UNSOS, and by extension threatening the existence of the AU mission, is a risk. It was probably for this reason that the U.S. backtracked in September to grant the UN mission an additional twelve months to draw down. But this move only defers rather than eliminates the challenges ahead. The U.S. argues that Mogadishu can keep Al-Shabaab at bay by enhancing the deployment of Somali forces, and combining this measure with assistance from abroad, including troops from neighbouring countries and air support from the U.S. and Türkiye. The U.S. says it remains ready to contribute to fighting Al-Shabaab. It just no longer wants to do so through a multilateral vehicle that it regards as an unnecessary expense. Are There Alternatives to UNSOS? The drawdown and eventual closure of UNSOS would, in effect, mean that the AU mission could not continue as currently designed. The UN mission keeps AU troops supplied with food, water and fuel, sustaining nearly 50 bases across southern Somalia. It also provides transport for AU deployments. When funds permit, it supports Somali soldiers operating alongside the AU personnel. Privately, AU officials say the mission cannot continue without UN support: one termed the U.S. decision on the UNOSOS mandate “life-threatening”. Even with a twelve-month stay of execution, the UN support office’s coming year will be focused on winding down its extensive logistical responsibilities. Deciding what comes next has become imperative for the Somali authorities. A few options for logistical assistance for the AU mission have been mooted, but all face serious drawbacks. In July, the Somali government, the AU and troop-contributing states met in the Ugandan capital Kampala to discuss the mission’s future. They endorsed a plan for uninterrupted support for another eighteen to 24 months, a period that would be used to carry out offensives against Al-Shabaab and a more gradual drawdown. For Washington, however, an extension of UN support beyond what is now on the table is out of the question, a stance it communicated in September. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. But given the AU’s lack of experience in running such a complex operation, this option appears unworkable in the near term. The AU could subcontract logistics to a private company, but diplomats note that it would take up to two years to establish a mission with capabilities similar to those of UNSOS. Even if it were possible, the financial crunch would not vanish. With the AU mission unable even to cover troop stipends, there is no way at present that it could shoulder the costs of logistics. The deeper pockets of partners alarmed by the possibility of an imminent worsening of Somali security, such as the EU or Gulf Arab countries, might be prised open to an extent. But with so many other crises competing for resources, a donor boost remains a long shot. Alternatively, the AU could take whatever funding is available from the EU and others, channelling it toward covering troop stipends and the logistics of a smaller mission. This option would enable the AU to maintain its presence, but only by sacrificing its operational clout, perhaps by retrenching at a few key locations, most likely in and around Mogadishu and regional capitals. But countries contributing troops to the AU mission already argue they do not have enough personnel to protect themselves, let alone undertake forward operations. Reducing their numbers further could end up at a point where the mission is unable to defend itself or others from Al-Shabaab attack. With limited funding committed for 2026 and nothing beyond that, the AU might also find it difficult to win donors over to the idea of supporting a less effective version of the same mission. A further variant of this option is being floated in Addis Ababa, where the AU has its headquarters: reconfiguring the mission under a new regional mechanism, but still with an AU mandate. In this scenario, many of the African troops deployed in Somalia would stay, but under a setup not unlike the Multinational Joint Task Force in the Lake Chad basin, a regional initiative to combat Boko Haram. Parallels with the Lake Chad basin are imperfect, however: the various national militaries operating there largely do so inside their own frontiers, coordinating more on cross-border matters. The proposal also offers little by way of a solution to the logistics and funding dilemmas, simply passing the buck to troop-contributing states. One or another of these options might emerge to enable Somalia’s multilateral security support to stagger on past 2027. The U.S. decision to grant an extra twelve months buys time to evaluate all the options and allows for less haste in the overhaul. But one way or another, a transition, with all its uncertainties, appears imminent. Turning to Somali Forces The AU’s exit strategy is premised on Somali forces standing ready to take the mission’s place when it finally shuts down. There is no doubt that the Somali National Army has boosted its strength in recent years, generating upward of 10,000 new troops under training schemes supported by foreign partners like Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates and Eritrea. But it is still ill-prepared to fully and rapidly take the AU mission’s place. Certain areas handed over by the mission to Somali forces in recent years have later fallen into Al-Shabaab’s hands. Even when the Somali army has led operations against Al-Shabaab, such as in Lower Shabelle in 2025-2026, it has remained dependent on external support. Somali officials have argued for many years that they can take full responsibility for security, but that they need more time. Many in the current government and its predecessors have wanted Somali forces to step up, only to find themselves hamstrung by political rifts within the federal system that have weakened the national security apparatus. State-level forces are generally underdeveloped, while the divisions between federal officials and leaders in Puntland and Jubaland, who are at loggerheads over how power and resources are divided in Somalia’s federal system, hinder the emergence of a unified national army. During times of political crisis, such as the election-related turmoil at present, federal and state forces sometimes turn their guns on each other. These shortcomings have driven Mogadishu to establish a series of bilateral security agreements with Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia, ensuring that their troops will stay despite the AU mission’s withdrawal. Uganda reportedly has a force of around 2,000 troops stationed in and around Mogadishu, while Kenya and Ethiopia retain larger contingents closer to their own borders. Bilateral foreign forces in Somalia have remained stable even as the AU mission shrinks, a trend that will probably continue after its eventual departure. What Could a New Security Approach Look Like? The AU mission’s future is for now unclear. While replacing support from the UN, and possibly finding a substitute for the mission, would undoubtedly be a huge undertaking, the situation is not hopeless. With proper planning, political leadership and a measure of continued foreign backing, the Somali government should be able to shift from dependence on a multilateral force to a series of bilateral relationships that prevent a major security breakdown and sweeping military gains by Al-Shabaab. That said, there is little doubt that the impending loss of the UN support office’s annual spending on Somali security needs will cause headaches. Even if the AU manages somehow to retain a presence, the most likely shape of Somalia’s future security support will derive chiefly from the deeply rooted interests of Mogadishu’s foreign partners. Key members of the AU mission, particularly Kenya and Ethiopia, are primarily motivated by border security, particularly the desire to maintain a buffer against Al-Shabaab. Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni views his country’s longstanding deployment as a key part of his legacy. He likely holds out hope that Mogadishu will be able to find a donor to pay for Ugandan units stationed around the capital. From outside the region, Türkiye has become Somalia’s most important bilateral partner in recent years, training thousands of Somali troops as well as deploying advanced military assets like drones and F-16s. Ankara also remains keen to protect its wide-ranging strategic investments in the country. The U.S., for its part, asserts that it will, for now, maintain its bilateral counter-terrorism operations, particularly its drone program. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes, regardless of what happens to the AU mission, while buying more time for the Somali military to assume greater responsibility. The AU mission’s major troop contributors would ideally keep most of their contingents where they are, arranging their own logistics in the process, but changes are likely. The loss of UNSOS assistance will probably spur Kenya and Ethiopia into consolidating positions nearer their own borders, while Uganda will probably focus more on protecting Mogadishu and its environs. Smaller troop contributors like Burundi and Djibouti, on the other hand, may be less inclined to continue without additional support. In areas where foreign troops do withdraw, Somali forces should prepare to take over. Mogadishu claimed in early August that it has 14,000 troops available for military operations, who could instead be deployed as holding forces to take the place of departing AU personnel. Somali troops tend not to be as well trained or equipped as their AU counterparts, however, making a one-to-one switch from AU to Somali soldiers a hazardous proposition. Taking these steps might contain Al-Shabaab to its rural bastions and avoid the loss of major cities. Proper coordination with bilateral forces could help protect the most strategically important areas, including towns, infrastructure and supply routes. But a modest fallback from some of the positions that are now under the AU mission’s control seems inevitable. Uganda, for example, maintains more than a dozen bases in the Lower Shabelle region, which will be difficult to hold without UNSOS logistical support. Smaller towns surrounded by Al-Shabaab, such as Qoryoley, could be at risk of falling to the insurgents once the AU pulls out. Parts of Hirshabelle would also be vulnerable due to the concentration of Al-Shabaab forces in the area since 2025, adding pressure to towns along the main road in the state, such as Jalalaqsi. Even small losses could give momentum back to Al-Shabaab, while the capture of roads and economic centres would help sustain the group financially. It may be possible over the coming years to keep parts of the battlefield tilted in the Somali authorities’ favour through the calibrated deployment of foreign troops, especially when it comes to the defence of urban centres and transport arteries. Still, the systemic challenges to Somali security thrown up by a radical change in security arrangements cannot be wished away. If they are left unaddressed, the danger will rise of greater government losses and an Al-Shabaab surge outside its rural strongholds. First, shifting the security burden onto African states will not resolve the funding problem unless donors and Somali officials take bold steps. If the AU wants to remain involved, it will have to do more to raise its own funds. If not, the AU mission’s current backers – primarily the EU and UK, which in 2025 together contributed approximately $90 million – could find ways to transfer this support to cover logistics and stipends for troop-contributing states from the region and Somali forces. Gulf Arab states, which number among Somalia’s key backers, may even be more inclined to support bilateral forces, viewing multilateral support as a poor investment because it translates into minimal diplomatic influence. Even though its resources are strained, the Somali government could also reduce the burden on foreign donors: the government has managed to raise domestic revenue in recent years and has even funded a number of internal military operations and deployments. The more it can take on, the less it will need to lobby the same donors on behalf of other African troop contributors. Secondly, the Somali government, troop-contributing countries and donors will need a forum in which to debate the country’s security needs and priorities. Security coordination within the AU mission has often proven a challenge, but the mission’s guiding framework helped ensure that its contributors adhered to a basic common strategy. The government should now establish a new forum that would meet regularly to coordinate with its bilateral partners, enabling Mogadishu to impress upon them the country’s main security requirements and hopefully curbing the pursuit of individual interests by troop-contributing states. Somalia’s security partners in turn should focus on fulfilling their security roles and avoid meddling in local politics in their areas of operation. A forum could also be an opportunity for the government to detail a national plan for Somalia’s future security, which would help assuage local concerns that a transition might leave some parts of the country better protected than others. Without effective coordination, bilateral security relationships could hasten the country’s fragmentation by fracturing it into various zones of influence that overlap with Somalia’s current divisions between the federal authorities and assertive member states. Furthermore, there is a risk that powerful partners might look to Mogadishu to provide exclusive concessions – economic or otherwise – in return for military assistance. Better coordination with multiple partners will help the Somali authorities handle these demands and keep the focus on making the country safe. With negotiations on the AU mission’s next mandate set to kick off at the UN Security Council by December, Somalia would benefit greatly from having a plan and buy-in from security partners in place by then. What Should Happen Now? Somalia’s multilateral security system has been limping toward its finale for several years. Establishing a new model without the UN support office and possibly the AU mission will be arduous; a series of bilateral security relationships is unlikely to match what multilateral deployments have achieved. Current funding and geopolitical realities, however, make this shift the most realistic option beyond 2027. The government should be using the time it has to make this change work. A clear grasp of the challenges ahead would be a good place to start. Diplomats from some of Mogadishu’s security partners say both the government and the AU expect that further compromises can be hammered out over the future of UNSOS. If so, that confidence is misplaced. The Trump administration appears intent on seeing the end of the UN support mission, even if it has signalled that more time is available to allow for a smoother transition. It is also hard to gauge how much UNSOS will be able to do in 2027 as it focuses on its liquidation. Rather than assume business as usual, Mogadishu and its partners should use the temporary reprieve they have been granted to construct a new security system that can kick into action as early as the second half of 2027. The Somali government should urgently convene its security partners to establish a broad division of responsibilities and priorities to follow the departure of UNSOS. Setting out a viable plan for the country after UN support winds down also has a better chance of attracting fresh donor backing. A shift primarily to bilateral support is still a temporary measure, and it should only buy time for a lasting solution to the country’s troubles: a Somali government that can manage its own security needs. Mogadishu’s shortcoming in achieving this goal, despite two decades of foreign support, is rooted in entrenched political divisions rather than just financial and technical challenges. In the short term, the government should be ready to deploy troops to areas likely to be vacated by foreign troops; it should launch major new offensives only once the transition has been consolidated. But for the security transition to work over the long term, Somalia’s government and political class must address their political divisions and row in the same direction. They could start to do so by resolving the dispute regarding the timing and format for elections, continuing by concluding these polls swiftly so that an incoming administration with a clear mandate can take office. The new administration should make preparing for a security transition an overriding priority. It should lay out a plan for how Somali forces can take over from foreign troops, including by bringing federal member states into discussions regarding the future of Somali security. Such a plan is the best way to realise the country’s full sovereignty – an oft-stated ambition of the Somali government. But the longer political disputes drag on, the greater the risk that the transition to Somali forces falters and Al-Shabaab resurges. The U.S. decision to pull the plug on UNSOS appears to be a defining act in the decline of Somalia’s multilateral security system. In its aftermath, short-term gains by Al-Shabaab look inevitable. But a well-managed transition should help mitigate any losses and lay the groundwork for Somalia’s eventual stability. Shrink the UN mloukili Mon, 09/21/2026 - 15:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Global 21 September 2026 1 minutes Shrink the UN Originally published in Foreign Affairs The Next Secretary-General Must Get Back to Basics Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Richard Gowan Program Director, Global Issues and Institutions https://twitter.com/RichardGowan1 Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy The United Nations, international officials sometimes joke, is always in crisis. Since its inception in 1945, the organization has had to navigate deep geopolitical tensions, devastating humanitarian disasters, and periodic budget shortfalls. But as world leaders gather in New York for the annual General Assembly high-level week, the UN appears to be in particularly bad shape. China, Russia, and the United States, three of the five veto-wielding powers that dominate the Security Council, have prevented it from acting on wars in Iran and Ukraine and civil conflicts in Myanmar and Sudan. Poor countries complain that donor states have not met their UN pledges on development spending. And the Trump administration halted most U.S. funding to UN activities last year, forcing the organization to cut back on its peacekeeping and relief efforts. With challenges mounting, an upcoming leadership transition may decide whether the UN can stabilize itself and perhaps even regain some credibility—or slide further into decrepitude. Current Secretary-General António Guterres plans to step down at the end of the year, having struggled to reverse the organization’s political fortunes in his decadelong tenure. He has spent much of his last two years in office grappling with staff reductions and other cost-cutting measures to ensure the UN secretariat does not go bankrupt on his watch. His has been a thankless task, but diplomats and UN officials hope a new leader will be able to take a longer-term approach to refreshing the institution and keeping governments committed to multilateralism. The small crop of candidates to succeed Guterres include senior UN trade official Rebeca Grynspan, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency Rafael Grossi, and Guyana’s Ambassador to the UN Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett. Regardless of who wins, Guterres' successor will need to develop a new playbook for revitalizing the organization. Any serious effort must acknowledge an unpleasant reality: as long as the world remains competitive and chaotic, the UN’s ability to forge wide-ranging international agreements will remain constrained. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/25/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. What Peacemaking Loses When Women Are Left Out cthuratong Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:39 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Gender and Conflict 25 September 2026 1 minute What Peacemaking Loses When Women Are Left Out Originally published in TIME Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Cristal Downing Project Director, Gender and Conflict https://twitter.com/cristaldowning?lang=en Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy Global Wars exact a heavy toll on women and yet, too often their voices and concerns are pushed to the margins of global peacemaking. Since the end of the Cold War, the United Nations has made halting but real progress in bringing women into peace negotiations and postwar reconstruction from Guatemala to Bangsamoro and beyond. Now that progress is being reversed. As peacemaking organizations fracture and lose their ability to press warring groups toward compromise, an assortment of social conservatives and warlords is finding new ways to exclude women from discussions about war and peace. Finding space for gender diversity could do more than ensure that women are heard; it could also give peace efforts a better chance of success. About a decade ago, Colombia’s peace process culminated in an agreement that seemed to offer a lesson in how to end a deeply rooted conflict. Negotiators brought in the belligerents but they also consulted civil society groups on rural reform, inclusive governance, and accountability for wartime atrocities, including sexual violence. Women’s groups had a voice in these discussions. The full article can be read on the TIME website. Arresting the Dangerous Descent Back into War in Northern Ethiopia eschelhaas Fri, 09/25/2026 - 14:01 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Members of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) walk along a main road in Mekelle on September 23, 2026, as tensions intensify in northern Ethiopia after Tigrayan rebels seized control of airports in the region. AFP Statement / Africa 25 September 2026 9 minutes Arresting the Dangerous Descent Back into War in Northern Ethiopia Long-simmering tensions have turned to large-scale fighting after armed opposition groups in Tigray, Amhara and Afar launched a multi-pronged offensive against Ethiopian government forces. It is not too late to avert a return to costly, bloody war. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Ethiopia Eritrea Northern Ethiopia is slipping into renewed war. After months of building tensions, on 23 September large-scale hostilities broke out between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and Amhara Fano militias, on one side, and the federal government and allied Tigrayan forces on the other. Responsibility for the escalation lies primarily with the TPLF, which launched ground assaults in coordination with other rebels with whom it has joined hands in a new alliance that vows to overthrow Ethiopia’s government. The upsurge in fighting comes almost five months after the TPLF retook power in the Tigray region, dealing a blow to a 2022 peace deal that had ended the last Tigray war and leading Addis Ababa to mount an intensifying drone campaign against TPLF forces. Much is unclear about how the two sides are faring on the battlefield, but many fear that further escalation in Tigray could draw in Eritrea, which is now closely aligned with the TPLF. Fighting in northern Ethiopia could also fuse dangerously with the war raging across the border in Sudan. African leaders backed by the U.S. and other outside powers should urge both sides to de-escalate and return to the negotiating table before hostilities spiral into a full-blown war that inflicts yet more suffering on civilians, while threatening to embroil other states. A Shaky Deal Gives Way The last war between the TPLF and Abiy’s federal government was one of the deadliest in the 21st century to date, killing hundreds of thousands. The roots of the conflict lie in the dramatic ascent of Abiy Ahmed to power in 2018. Abiy’s political base is in the Oromia region. His rise to the premiership ended the TPLF’s heavy-handed rule, and its decades-long political dominance, but also presaged a new struggle to come. TPLF leaders decamped to Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle to regroup. Full-scale war erupted in 2020, when TPLF forces launched a surprise attack on the federal military’s northern command post. Momentum swung both ways before Abiy and his coalition gained the upper hand in 2022. Under heavy military pressure, the TPLF agreed to a deal in November of that year ending the fighting. Under that accord, signed in Pretoria, the TPLF promised to disarm, and the parties agreed that Tigray would have an interim administration governing with the approval of both sides. While welcomed for bringing the conflict to an end, the Pretoria deal left a number of open wounds. While welcomed for bringing the conflict to an end, the Pretoria deal left a number of open wounds . The TPLF felt aggrieved by what it considered a lopsided settlement and, according to the government, it failed to honour its disarmament pledge. Eritrea, which had overcome enmity with the federal government to join the anti-TPLF campaign, felt it had been inadequately consulted on the final deal and wished the government had pushed to achieve a full battlefield victory. The status of hotly contested territories that the Amhara region had seized from Tigray during the conflict was left unresolved – leaving Tigrayans displaced from these areas languishing in temporary camps. Shoring up the wobbly settlement would have required patient statecraft from outside actors pressing the former belligerents to compromise, but the diplomacy that occurred was unavailing. Instead, the deal slowly collapsed. In late April and early May, the TPLF ousted Tigray’s interim administration and reinstalled its head Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president. After wresting back control of the region, TPLF leaders launched a major conscription drive and made a series of comments suggesting that their goal is to remove Abiy from power. They also repeatedly warned of an imminent return to war. Dialogue between the TPLF and other key rebel groups to form an alliance also accelerated, though these groups have little in common besides opposition to the government. The federal government, which was already cutting off federal funds and restricting fuel to the region as relations with the TPLF went into a rapid decline, began to launch occasional drone strikes on targets in Tigray. Shuttle diplomacy between Addis Ababa and Mekelle by the African Union’s envoy, former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who oversaw the 2022 peace talks, appeared to make little progress toward direct negotiations or an off-ramp. Regional tensions further poisoned the waters. Fuelled by its bitterness over the Pretoria agreement, and in line with the byzantine nature of alliance building in the region, Eritrea is now quietly aligned with its former enemy the TPLF. Meanwhile, Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of playing a central role in coordinating the opposition alliance that has formed against it. There is also a Sudan angle. Ethiopia’s leaders are furious at the Sudanese army for hosting thousands of Tigrayan fighters in territory under its control, whom they fear could attack Ethiopia from across the border or return to Tigray to join in battling the government. Many of these fighters have aided Khartoum in its own civil war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Seeing the Sudanese army as part of a regional axis coordinating with Ethiopian opposition forces, Addis Ababa has reportedly responded by allowing arms flows to the RSF and permitting it to operate from Ethiopian territory near Sudan’s Blue Nile state, where the paramilitary has made a series of gains. Ethiopia is also a close ally of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which is widely seen (despite its denials) as the RSF’s main backer. Meanwhile, the UAE’s Saudi rivals are aligned with the Sudanese army, as are Egypt and Eritrea, both arch-foes of Ethiopia. Diplomats and mediators say the superheated regional climate – in which both continental and Gulf powers are lining up on different sides of the Horn’s overlapping conflicts – has made it an uphill struggle to ward off a return to war in northern Ethiopia. Growing Tensions and a Return to War Tensions only increased over the course of August and September. As the culmination of its coalition-building efforts, on 20 September, the TPLF announced it was forming an Alliance for Survival with six other groups, most prominently a major umbrella organisation of the Amhara Fano rebel movement, which launched an insurgency against the government in August 2023. A statement launching the alliance set out its objective as overthrowing Abiy’s government . Then, on 22 September, the federal government responded with its biggest drone attack since August, targeting an apparent build-up of Tigrayan forces close to the Wollo area of the Amhara region where several anti-government groups are active. By 23 September, large-scale ground fighting between the TPLF and government forces had begun, with the former taking over three Tigray airports that had been still under federal control in Mekelle and the major towns of Axum and Shire, replacing the federal police stationed with their own forces without a fight. The federal government cancelled all flights to the Tigray region. The multi-front offensive appears to be the first attempt by the new opposition alliance to carry out coordinated military action against the federal government. Fighting in the north is now concentrated in two main areas. One is in the Amhara region close to the boundary with Southern Tigray, where Tigrayan forces and Amhara Fano launched a ground assault on federal forces on 23 September. The other hotspot is the boundary between Tigray and the Afar region to the east, where on the same day the TPLF launched an offensive against the government-backed anti-TPLF armed group the Tigray Peace Forces. Adding another combustible element, an anti-government group from Afar also joined the fray, fighting alongside the TPLF in two locations on the Tigray-Afar border. The multi-front offensive appears to be the first attempt by the new opposition alliance to carry out coordinated military action against the federal government. Government officials and several diplomats blamed the TPLF for the erupting conflict. Getachew Reda, the former senior Tigrayan official who is now an adviser to Abiy, accused the TPLF of starting a new war. The U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia, Ervin Massinga, also put out a statement expressing “disappointment” with the “large-scale offensive” launched by the TPLF. Other sources in Ethiopia appear to confirm that the TPLF launched the major new assaults, in coordination with other groups. In a statement , the TPLF claimed that its actions were “defensive” in nature, responding to the government’s “open invasion” on 22 September when it launched its barrage of drone strikes on Tigrayan military targets. Situation Report At the time of publication, the heaviest fighting is centred in the North Wollo area in the Amhara region, near the boundary with Tigray, where the TPLF and Fano elements appear to be coordinating their offensive against federal positions. With the Tigrayans and Fano reportedly taking territory and threatening several major towns in northern parts of Amhara, including Weldiya and Lalibela, all eyes are on the federal government’s response. The situation looks set to deteriorate as the government throws more troops and weaponry at beating back the TPLF and its allies, though few believe the opposition groups have the punch to pose a direct threat to the federal authorities in Addis Ababa. Should the government manage to halt or reverse the offensives beyond Tigray, a key question will then be whether Addis Ababa launches a large-scale ground war to remove the TPLF from power in Mekelle and restore federal control of most of Tigray. Privately, a senior government official stated that Addis Ababa will now seek to eliminate the TPLF as a threat, though another official suggested that the government would prefer to avoid a full-fledged war. To date, Abiy has appeared hesitant to get sucked into such a war in Tigray, but he may decide he has little alternative. Beyond the risk of setting off an unpredictable spiral, a major escalation could also push the fighting close to the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, creating the potential for interstate conflict. There is also a risk of conflict erupting along the Sudan-Ethiopia border, in effect merging the two countries’ conflicts, given the federal government’s and TPLF’s ties to rival belligerents there. A major incursion into Tigray by the federal government would also almost assuredly lead to extensive destruction, displacement and mass casualties – in short, a humanitarian disaster. Key African leaders ... as well as past and present heads of state ... should urgently push both sides to de-escalate and pursue an off-ramp into direct talks. Given the bad blood between the Ethiopian belligerents, outside engagement in the form of high-level diplomacy will likely be needed to prevent a plunge back into all-out conflict. Many have a role to play. Key African leaders, including Obasanjo (in his capacity as the AU’s High Representative for the Horn of Africa), as well as past and present heads of state, such as Kenyan President William Ruto and former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, should urgently push both sides to de-escalate and pursue an off-ramp into direct talks. These leaders should urge the TPLF to halt its offensives and take its grievances to the negotiating table, while they should also engage with Abiy to avoid a major new ground invasion of Tigray and to allow time for emergency diplomacy. By way of support, Saudi Arabia should push its allies in Asmara, Khartoum and Cairo, all of which have significant disputes with Addis Ababa, to avoid meddling and further inflaming the situation. For its part, the UAE should press its allies in Addis Ababa toward diplomacy and avoid fanning the flames with large new arms transfers. The U.S., which has shuttled between Addis and Mekelle and backed Obasanjo’s mediation, as well as key European powers, should back all these efforts through their own continued outreach, including to the traditionally highly insular Eritrean government. Averting a Nightmare Scenario With wars already raging nearby in Somalia, Sudan and Yemen, not to mention those beyond, a major new conflict in Ethiopia is a nightmare scenario. The humanitarian consequences are potentially horrific – all the more so given what northern Ethiopia has already experienced in recent years – and there is a non-trivial risk that other countries get dragged into what could become a regional conflagration . A window is still open for averting these outcomes – but absent urgent diplomacy, it could close all too soon. Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. Central African Republic: ICC Verdict in Seleka Commander Case. Click to expand Image Mahamat Said Abdel Kani during closing statements in the courtroom of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, November 25, 2025. © 2025 ICC-CPi (The Hague) – The International Criminal Court (ICC)’s conviction of Mahamat Said Abdel Kani for crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic offers an important measure of long-awaited justice for victims of the abusive Seleka armed group, Human Rights Watch said today. In 2012, the predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels ousted the Central African Republic president, François Bozizé, and seized power through a campaign of violence and terror. In March 2013, the Seleka took control of Bangui, the capital, attacking civilians and pillaging the city. In late 2013, Christian and animist militias known as anti-balaka, began to organize counterattacks against the Seleka. Both the Seleka and anti-balaka have been implicated in widespread atrocities against civilians. “As the first ICC verdict against a high-level Seleka commander, the judgment against Said is a significant milestone in the fight against impunity for serious crimes in the Central African Republic,” said Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “But this should only be considered a first step. The verdict is also a stark reminder of the ongoing abuses in the country, and the need for increased support for both international and domestic justice efforts to end the accountability gap that helps fuel recurring cycles of violence.” ICC judges convicted Said for crimes committed at the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry (Office Central de Répression du Banditisme, OCRB) in Bangui between April and August 2013. The crimes include imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty, torture, other inhumane acts, and persecution. Said was acquitted on the charges of war crimes. The majority of the judges found that the ouster of François Bozizé in March 2013 ended the conflict that had begun between the Seleka and the Central African armed forces in 2012, and therefore, there was no conflict at the time the alleged crimes were committed. Said was also acquitted for some incidents related to the crimes against humanity charges, including for lack of sufficient evidence. The court laid out a timeline for the sentencing proceedings, which will include a hearing in November. The court should take all necessary steps to ensure that affected communities in the Central African Republic learn about the judgment and next steps, including any appeals and reparations proceedings, Human Rights Watch said. Said is believed to have joined the Seleka in 2012 and was promoted to lieutenant, colonel, and then commander. In April 2013, when Seleka abuse in Bangui was acute, he was given a key role in the Central Office for the Repression of Banditry. The agency is a police unit created in the late 1990s to address a rise in banditry, which developed a reputation for abuse. Its abuse continues today and the government uses the unit at times to warn government critics of potential consequences of their criticism. Said was arrested in the Central African Republic and surrendered to the ICC on January 24, 2021. The court’s judges had issued an under-seal arrest warrant against him on January 7, 2019. In 2014, the Seleka splintered into several groups, including the Popular Front for the Renaissance (Front populaire pour la renaissance de la Centrafrique, FPRC), headed by Noureddine Adam and Michel Djotodia. Some factions of the FPRC aligned themselves with anti-balaka forces. Djotodia, who is sanctioned by the US Treasury, lives in Benin but returned to Bangui in 2020 for a short stay and is sometimes back in the country. Adam is reported to be between Chad and Sudan, where he continues to evade justice. On July 28, 2022, the ICC unsealed an arrest warrant against Adam, which was first issued against him under seal on January 7, 2019. ICC member countries should make every effort to support the court in arresting Adam and bring him to justice, Human Rights Watch said. Other high-profile Seleka leaders, such as Mahamat Al Khatim, Saleh Zabadi, and Ali Darassa, continue to lead splinter Seleka groups. In July 2025, ICC judges convicted two anti-balaka leaders, Alfred Yékatom and Patrice-Edouard Ngaïssona, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Central African Republic between December 2013 and August 2014. Yékatom and Ngaïssona were sentenced to 15 and 12 years in prison, respectively, and appeals are ongoing. Another anti-balaka commander, Maxim Mokom, was surrendered to the court in March 2022, but the prosecution withdrew the charges against him in October 2023, citing a lack of evidence and witnesses. The ICC opened the investigation into crimes committed in the Central African Republic since 2012, following a request from the Central African Republic government in 2014. This was the ICC’s second investigation into crimes committed in the country. The first investigation related to an earlier conflict, in 2002 and 2003, and resulted in the acquittal of Jean-Pierre Bemba, a former vice president from the Democratic Republic of Congo. In December 2022, the ICC prosecutor announced the completion of his office’s investigative activities in the Central African Republic. ICC investigations in the Central African Republic have been complemented by proceedings before the Special Criminal Court in Bangui, staffed by international and Central African judges and prosecutors. The court has issued verdicts in four cases and has several ongoing proceedings and investigations. This critical justice avenue is facing significant financial challenges. International partners should provide the court with the resources it needs to fulfill its important mandate, Human Rights Watch said. Said’s verdict comes at a time when the ICC is facing extreme pressure. In February 2025, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order authorizing sanctions on ICC officials and others supporting the court’s work. Since then, the US government has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and staff, a UN expert, and three leading Palestinian human rights organizations. Together with three other human rights groups, Human Rights Watch has sued the Trump administration in a US court over its sanctions targeting the ICC. On July 13, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced an escalated campaign to “dismantle” the court, including an increased use of sanctions and pressure on ICC member countries to leave the court. “The ICC is a critical court of last resort to deliver justice for the most serious crimes in the Central African Republic and across its docket,” Mudge said. “ICC member countries should redouble their efforts to protect the ICC and those supporting its work, so it can deliver on its essential global mandate.”

Russia Crackdown on Bypassing Online Censorship. Click to expand Image A person checks their phone in the Red Square in Moscow, Russia, March 31, 2026. © 2026 Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo (Berlin, September 24, 2026) – Russian authorities are doubling down on their efforts to quash freedom of expression, including access to information, by increasingly suppressing tools to circumvent draconian censorship laws, Human Rights Watch said today. Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) services face intensifying blocking and takedowns from app stores. “The Russian government’s escalating attacks on censorship circumvention services is part of its broader assault on access to information, privacy, and freedom of expression,” said Hugh Williamson, Europe and Central Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “These repressive tactics affect millions of people in Russia seeking to connect to the internet without state censorship.” On August 4, 2026, Exploit media outlet reported that 20 Virtual Private Network (VPN) providers in Russia had faced service disruptions caused by the blockings carried out by the Russian authorities. A representative of one of the affected VPN services told Human Rights Watch that the recent waves of blocking targeted VPN services’ infrastructure, namely, large blocks of IP addresses they use, including entire subnets of IP addresses allocated to them by their hosting service providers. Restoring VPN services following such bulk blocking can take more time and be more costly in comparison to previous more granular state blocking, the representative said. In June, the authorities carried out a coordinated attack targeting Amnezia VPN, one of the most popular VPN services in Russia. One of Amnezia’s developers said that the authorities blocked its IP addresses in bulk, targeted employees with phishing emails in an attempt to obtain sensitive data, and used distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks, which overwhelmed the service and disrupted its work. It took Amnezia one and a half months to fully restore its services. The new tactics in state crackdown on VPNs have created significant technical, financial, and operational challenges and damaged their reputation as reliable services, Human Rights Watch said. In April, the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media instructed more than 20 of the largest internet companies, which together provide digital services to the vast majority of Russians, to gather information on their clients’ VPN use and deny access to services when detecting VPN connections. According to a study published by RKS Global, a group of experts working on internet freedom, at least 30 of the largest Russian apps gathered this information. An expert at RKS Global told Human Rights Watch that the information included IP addresses used by the VPN services and was used in the recent attack on VPNs’ infrastructure. Over the past decade, VPNs have become a lifeline for accessing millions of censored websites in Russia, including to access independent media, foreign social media and messaging platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, and WhatsApp. Since spring 2025, the authorities have increasingly carried out “whitelists” shutdowns, blocking access to all but state approved websites. The 2017 law on VPN services prohibited them from providing access to state-blocked websites. By February 2026, the authorities had blocked at least 469 VPNs under this law.
